articles.title: A final surge: On Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s triumph in Brazil
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Lula is the resistance to U.S. imperial ambitions in South America

At one point, it seemed almost impossible for Brazil’s 80-year-old President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to turn the tide after finishing second to Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of elections on October 4. In Brazil’s history, no candidate who has finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidential run-off. Most of the candidates who dropped out after the first round were from the right. Flávio’s Liberal Party cemented its position in both houses of Congress, while right-wing candidates won several provincial elections. But Lula, a former trade unionist and organiser, who lost a finger in an accident as a teenager, was not ready to give up. Lula and his Workers’ Party identified campaign weaknesses, shifted their attention to economic issues, promised growth and welfare, and persuaded more voters to turn out for Sunday’s run-off. Lula won 51.7% of the vote against Flávio’s 48.2%, a greater lead than his victory against Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio’s father, four years ago. Over the weeks, Lula turned the right-wing’s gains in the first round against it, highlighting the threats that a Bolsonaro victory could pose to democracy and civil rights. Flávio’s campaign pledge to free his father — he is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn Lula’s 2022 victory, and impeach Supreme Court judges — only heightened the concerns of voters outside the right wing, who rallied behind a familiar face.

Lula unleashed a social media campaign to mobilise younger voters. A WhatsApp channel called ‘Lula’s Army’ with 11 million followers spread his message of continuity. He also announced plans to expand a cash payout scheme for the poor, a new debt relief package and entrepreneur-friendly measures. In the northeast, the Workers’ Party’s stronghold, he gained nearly three million votes and made considerable gains in the working-class neighbourhoods of big cities, including São Paulo. A relatively stable economic record, marked by growth and falling unemployment over the past three and a half years, also lent credibility to Lula’s appeal. His victory bucks the recent trend in South America, where Washington-aligned right-wing and conservative forces have gained ground. While Lula offers predictable stability and social and economic inclusiveness, he could also be, as the President of South America’s largest economy, a voice of resistance to Donald Trump’s imperial ambitions. At the same time, Lula will have to work with a right-wing-controlled Congress to advance his agenda. He should seek to build legislative consensus while focusing on addressing the economic challenges of Brazil, which remains one of the most unequal major world economies.

articles.title: Dubious retreat: On the National Medical Commission and its MSMER
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The National Medical Commission must not be seen as lax on regulation

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has denotified and withdrawn its 2023 Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations (MSMER ), diminishing the framework of penalties vis-à-vis educational standards and infrastructure at medical colleges. The move is noteworthy as the MSMER provided for fines of up to ₹5 lakh on faculty members and administrators for submitting false information. Fortunately, the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) retains the power to fine errant institutions up to ₹1 crore under the 2023 Establishment of Medical Institutions, Assessment and Rating Regulations . MSMER was lauded for its intention to crack down on the deep-seated corruption and malpractice in medical colleges, particularly over ‘ghost faculty’ and ‘ghost patients’. The NMC’s justification is that MSMER also introduced a parallel mechanism allowing undergraduate and postgraduate boards to evaluate institutions, stepping on the MARB’s toes. However, why the NMC scrapped MSMER wholesale is unclear. The 2023 Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations remain in force and include a provision to fine individual faculty members at postgraduate medical colleges. Non-compliance among medical colleges is not uncommon and seldom nipped in the bud, even as the number of medical seats swells while the transparency of the medical education system has not improved.

Notwithstanding the provision to fine individuals at postgraduate centres, the MARB and the NMC can only penalise institutions, which is harder and risks creating a perverse incentive to accommodate rather than punish, and could mitigate the fear that keeps administrators honest. MSMER also specified timelines to appeal penalties. Although the MARB regulations retain the appeal processes, their 15-day deadline could conflict with the 60-day period under the NMC Act, potentially creating legal disputes that delay penal action. There is also a telling incident. As part of a proceeding under the RTI Act, the Central Information Commission revealed last year that the NMC had stated in 2024 that MARB had neither formally assessed nor rated medical colleges and that its standard forms need not be made public. In a revised reply in October 2025, it said the responding NMC officer’s records did not include any of the corresponding reports. However, the 2023 MARB regulations require the Board to publish its latest annual assessment results. If the NMC withdrew MSMER because the powers thereunder also exist elsewhere, the public deserves to know whether the powers are also being exercised and whether the outcomes are as publicly accessible as intended. Unless the NMC has satisfactory answers for all these lacunae, the withdrawal will appear less like simplification and more like regulatory relaxation.

articles.title: Wicked surprise: On the northeast monsoon
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The northeast monsoon is more unpredictable, and the south must be wary

As India recovers from a monsoon-deficit year , there is both hope and trepidation regarding the prospects for that ‘other monsoon’, or the ‘northeast monsoon’ . While contributing only around a quarter of India’s annual rainfall, it is largely focused on the south-east peninsula regions of Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, coastal Andhra Pradesh, Rayalaseema, south interior Karnataka and Keralam. The southwest monsoon, influenced by a strengthening El Niño , has already left its desiccating mark. Rainfall from June-September was 759.4 mm against 868.6 mm, a 12.6% deficit, the driest in 11 years. This has impacted kharif sowing and is reflected in food inflation.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has said that this year, the northeast monsoon rainfall, spanning October to December, would likely be ‘normal’ , meaning in line with a 50-year average and within a 12% error window. Most parts of the country, it said, are expected to receive below-normal rainfall, except some areas of northwest India and southern parts of peninsular India, where rainfall is likely to be normal to above-normal. The wide error window, however, is far less precise than its forecasts for the southwest monsoon with its margin of 5%, and can sometimes make the northeast monsoon the bearer of nasty surprises. For instance, December 1, 2015, saw the city of Chennai deluged by its heaviest rainfall in 24-hours in over a century ; at least 500 lives were lost and 18 lakh people displaced in the State. That year and the present are linked by a common thread: a powerful El Niño. Associated with the heating up of the Central Pacific, the El Niño is linked to the drying up of the southwest monsoon rains but also yoked — not always — with a vigorous northeast monsoon. Other than in 2015, several El Niño years, such as 1997 and 2009, have been associated with above-normal rainfall between October and December in Tamil Nadu though El Niño years, such as 2002 and 1982, saw a poor northeast monsoon (and a predictably bad southwest monsoon). While the climate mechanisms linking a vigorous northeast monsoon and El Niño are still to be fully understood, it appears the warming patterns of the El Niño tend to deflect rain-bearing cyclonic circulations in unpredictable ways. Therefore, the Centre and the southern States ought to take enough precautions: from clearing up stormwater drains, fortifying shelters, making provisions for infrastructure damage and tightening weather warning forecasts to prepare for torrents.

• The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has said that this year, the northeast monsoon rainfall, spanning October to December, would likely be ‘normal’ , meaning in line with a 50-year average and within a 12% error window. Most parts of the country, it said, are expected to receive below-normal rainfall, except some areas of northwest India and southern parts of peninsular India, where rainfall is likely to be normal to above-normal. The wide error window, however, is far less precise than its forecasts for the southwest monsoon with its margin of 5%, and can sometimes make the northeast monsoon the bearer of nasty surprises. For instance, December 1, 2015, saw the city of Chennai deluged by its heaviest rainfall in 24-hours in over a century ; at least 500 lives were lost and 18 lakh people displaced in the State. That year and the present are linked by a common thread: a powerful El Niño. Associated with the heating up of the Central Pacific, the El Niño is linked to the drying up of the southwest monsoon rains but also yoked — not always — with a vigorous northeast monsoon. Other than in 2015, several El Niño years, such as 1997 and 2009, have been associated with above-normal rainfall between October and December in Tamil Nadu though El Niño years, such as 2002 and 1982, saw a poor northeast monsoon (and a predictably bad southwest monsoon). While the climate mechanisms linking a vigorous northeast monsoon and El Niño are still to be fully understood, it appears the warming patterns of the El Niño tend to deflect rain-bearing cyclonic circulations in unpredictable ways. Therefore, the Centre and the southern States ought to take enough precautions: from clearing up stormwater drains, fortifying shelters, making provisions for infrastructure damage and tightening weather warning forecasts to prepare for torrents.

Sixteen years after his visit as Poland’s Prime Minister, Donald Tusk’s travel to Delhi and Bengaluru last week was to signal a renewed desire to work closely with India. Mr. Tusk’s visit, two months ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s trip to Brussels to sign the India-European Union (EU) Free Trade Agreement , indicated one part of his agenda. Both sides agreed that it was time to develop trade, currently worth just $6 billion, to double its size by 2030. Mr. Tusk’s last visit to India was in 2017, as President of the European Council for the EU-India summit, and it is fitting that his trip was just as the FTA is finalised and ratified after years of delays. Another area of increased India-Poland collaboration is in technology, AI and defence hardware, critical minerals, renewable and nuclear energy given Poland’s expertise in the last few decades and India’s capacity for scale. As the EU’s sixth largest economy, Poland has officially crossed the $1 trillion GDP (nominal terms) milestone. Its $120-billion-dollar tech economy is also gaining global interest. A large part of Polish machinery and parts is exported to Germany, which in turn has a growing share of Indian imports, and India could consider more trilateral collaborations for manufacturing and mining technology. The two sides agreed to establish a “Defence Industry Dialogue” and explore a dialogue on counter-terrorism cooperation. Finally, the Modi-Tusk talks focused on geopolitics, particularly the ongoing war in Ukraine. The war’s impact, especially on the Global South, has been a concern for India, and the Modi government’s initiative to work on an agreement acceptable to Kyiv and Moscow on grain exports and seafarers’ safety was discussed. The four-pronged plan, announced by External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar during his September visit to Warsaw, won Mr. Tusk’s support.

At the India-Poland Business Forum in Bengaluru, Mr. Tusk, who was accompanied by a Polish business delegation, said the challenge now was in “translating” the talks and MoUs signed into actual joint ventures between businesses. Apart from the distance and geographies, there is the matter of trust, given India’s defence engagement with Russia and Poland’s defence ties with Pakistan. Poland is credited with training Pakistan’s Air Force in its early years; a mutual defence cooperation agreement was signed in 2018. India has a unique and enduring partnership with Russia, and New Delhi is unlikely to accept Warsaw’s strictures over its military engagement and exercises with Russia that caused a controversy earlier this year during the Polish Foreign Minister’s visit. It is essential for Delhi and Warsaw to complete the confidentiality of classified information that is still being negotiated and draw up the parameters of future cooperation based on realities. Mr. Tusk’s statement that India and Poland today have no “conflicts of interest” is a significant aspiration, for two countries that share old values, and new avenues of partnership.

articles.title: In the crossfire: on India and the Saudi-Houthi conflict
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: India must adopt a pro-active position in the Saudi-Houthi conflict

The killing of an Indian national in a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport is a grim reminder of the dangers the kingdom’s Indian community faces as the conflict between Riyadh and Yemen’s Shia militants escalates. Since the fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed in July, at least two Indians have been killed and 14 others wounded. On Thursday, the Houthis claimed that a yacht with 14 Indians was targeted by Saudi forces near Yemen’s Zuqar island in the Red Sea and that rescue operations were under way. As the Houthis, who control parts of Northern Yemen and its entire Red Sea coast, step up attacks on Saudi infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports, Indians, who are the kingdom’s largest expat community, risk getting caught in the crossfire. With flights disrupted, thousands of Indian pilgrims are stranded. India has condemned Houthi attacks, saying that it “stands in solidarity” with Saudi Arabia. With no end in sight to the fighting and a high possibility of Israel and the U.S. resuming their Iran strikes, further violence and instability in West Asia could make India’s choices increasingly difficult.

The Saudi-Houthi conflict dates back to the Houthi takeover of Sana’a, Yemen’s capital, in 2014. A year later, Saudi Arabia began bombing Yemen to drive the Houthis out. But years of Saudi bombing of one of the poorest Arab countries have proved counterproductive; the Houthis consolidated support among the tribes of northern Yemen and built a powerful territorial army and naval force. The Saudi-Houthi ceasefire of 2022 collapsed in July 2026 after Saudi Arabia recklessly bombed Sana’a airport, to prevent an Iranian plane with a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis subsequently began attacking Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure, and launched a ground offensive against the Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. The Houthi attacks pose the biggest security challenge to Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince and the main architect of the war on Yemen, in decades. Massive Saudi air strikes have neither defeated the Houthis nor restored the kingdom’s deterrence. With its wealth, natural resources, infrastructure and tenuous palace politics, the kingdom remains exposed to Houthi missile and drone attacks, with few good options for a way out. India must prepare a contingency plan for worst-case scenarios. Its immediate priority should be to evacuate stranded Indian pilgrims. It should also articulate a stronger position for stability and work with Arab countries and Tehran to push for a diplomatic settlement to the Iran crisis . For peace to prevail in the Persian Gulf, the guns directed at Iran must first fall silent.

articles.title: Falling short: on Marco Rubio’s second visit to India
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Marco Rubio’s second visit to India this year yielded little in terms of results

The United States Secretary of State’s three-day visit to India , his second in five months, came at a significant time in U.S. politics. Marco Rubio’s Mumbai trip this week was just ahead of the U.S. midterm elections , which would mark the midpoint of President Donald Trump’s second term in office — a point at which the incumbent normally begins to focus on legacy, and possible contenders for the next Presidential election (Mr. Rubio is expected to be one), and start to look for possible partners and friendships around the world. In addition, his visit also raised hopes in New Delhi of a reset in bilateral ties, battered by two years of uncertainty over the Trump administration’s actions. This would include positive moves towards concluding the Bilateral Trade Agreement , reassuring India about U.S. sanctions on the import of Russian oil, preparations for upcoming Trump meets with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Manila (ASEAN) and Miami (G-20) summits, discussing plans for the Quad Summit (on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit) that India has been trying to host, and setting a date for Mr. Trump’s India visit. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar’s invitation also offered Mr. Rubio an opportunity to meet their UAE counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, to discuss the Gulf situation and to restore energy security and connectivity. And finally, Mr. Rubio’s visit to the Jamnagar Reliance refinery, led to speculation of some major deals on energy, possibly offering more discounts as he pitched for India to buy more American and U.S.-licensed Venezuelan oil.

Given all the high expectations, the visit was bound to come up short. The optics of his visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar, but not New Delhi, which was announced by the U.S. Ambassador to India , gave the Opposition fodder to question the real purpose of the visit. Despite Mr. Rubio’s two visits to India and more than six by Mr. Jaishankar to the U.S. since Mr. Trump took office, relations remain on edge, with issues on trade, tariffs, H-1B restrictions and anti-immigrant measures unaddressed. Also, the U.S.’s narrative on Operation Sindoor (2025), growing ties with Pakistan, and the Trump administration’s rhetoric on India’s economy, diaspora and Russian oil trade have added to India’s unhappiness. The two sides did not announce any agreements and Mr. Jaishankar and Mr. Rubio did not hold a joint press address. However, as they did at the U.S. Independence Day’s 250th anniversary celebrations in Delhi in May, they attended the “Freedom 250” event in Mumbai. Mr. Rubio acknowledged that while no two countries would agree on all issues, he said the U.S.-India alignment on core issues of national interest was “extraordinary” . From this point on, Mr. Rubio must walk that talk, with a view to ensuring that India-U.S. ties are able to move on from the difficulties of the last few years.

The United States Secretary of State’s three-day visit to India , his second in five months, came at a significant time in U.S. politics. Marco Rubio’s Mumbai trip this week was just ahead of the U.S. midterm elections , which would mark the midpoint of President Donald Trump’s second term in office — a point at which the incumbent normally begins to focus on legacy, and possible contenders for the next Presidential election (Mr. Rubio is expected to be one), and start to look for possible partners and friendships around the world. In addition, his visit also raised hopes in New Delhi of a reset in bilateral ties, battered by two years of uncertainty over the Trump administration’s actions. This would include positive moves towards concluding the Bilateral Trade Agreement , reassuring India about U.S. sanctions on the import of Russian oil, preparations for upcoming Trump meets with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Manila (ASEAN) and Miami (G-20) summits, discussing plans for the Quad Summit (on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit) that India has been trying to host, and setting a date for Mr. Trump’s India visit. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar’s invitation also offered Mr. Rubio an opportunity to meet their UAE counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, to discuss the Gulf situation and to restore energy security and connectivity. And finally, Mr. Rubio’s visit to the Jamnagar Reliance refinery, led to speculation of some major deals on energy, possibly offering more discounts as he pitched for India to buy more American and U.S.-licensed Venezuelan oil.

Given all the high expectations, the visit was bound to come up short. The optics of his visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar, but not New Delhi, which was announced by the U.S. Ambassador to India , gave the Opposition fodder to question the real purpose of the visit. Despite Mr. Rubio’s two visits to India and more than six by Mr. Jaishankar to the U.S. since Mr. Trump took office, relations remain on edge, with issues on trade, tariffs, H-1B restrictions and anti-immigrant measures unaddressed. Also, the U.S.’s narrative on Operation Sindoor (2025), growing ties with Pakistan, and the Trump administration’s rhetoric on India’s economy, diaspora and Russian oil trade have added to India’s unhappiness. The two sides did not announce any agreements and Mr. Jaishankar and Mr. Rubio did not hold a joint press address. However, as they did at the U.S. Independence Day’s 250th anniversary celebrations in Delhi in May, they attended the “Freedom 250” event in Mumbai. Mr. Rubio acknowledged that while no two countries would agree on all issues, he said the U.S.-India alignment on core issues of national interest was “extraordinary” . From this point on, Mr. Rubio must walk that talk, with a view to ensuring that India-U.S. ties are able to move on from the difficulties of the last few years.

articles.title: Notify Pallikaranai under Wetlands Rules, 2017: Sowmiya Anbumani
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: She alleges that the CMDA’s approval of buildings over natural drainage channels and waterways is itself a serious violation of the law

PMK floor leader Sowmiya Anbumani on Tuesday urged the Tamil Nadu State Wetlands Authority to immediately notify Pallikaranai marshland under the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017, and include all 65 water bodies flowing into the marshlands within its zone of influence.

In a letter submitted to Rakesh Kumar Jageniya, Member Secretary, Tamil Nadu State Wetlands Authority in Chennai, Ms. Sowmiya demanded that the newly constructed compound wall and walkway on the marshland be removed.
Aerial view of Pallikaranai marshland, a Ramsar site. | Photo Credit: JOTHI RAMALINGAM B

“Construction companies planning to build large structures in the zone of influence of Pallikaranai Ramsar Wetland appear to want to block the waterways that bring water to the wetland and prevent the flow of water so that they can construct buildings. Several major construction companies have already built structures over drainage channels, leaving passages beneath the buildings for water to flow. The CMDA’s approval of buildings over natural drainage channels and waterways is itself a serious violation of the law,” she charged.

Major construction companies are reportedly planning to encroach upon areas surrounding the 65 water bodies in the Pallikaranai watershed, as well as the channels through which the water flows. “This could well be the real reason why construction companies are demanding a reduction in the area designated as the zone of influence of the wetland. A wetland and its zone of influence are not the same. Under the 2017 Rules, permanent construction is prohibited within the notified wetland boundary. The same blanket prohibition does not apply to the zone of influence outside the wetland,” she said.

articles.title: ECI’s stand that additional declaration is not part of Form 6 comes days after SC said it will examine ‘new’ Form 6
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The ECI has introduced an additional declaration form along with Form 6 which require these voters to provide details of their earlier electoral roll entries or that of their parents or grandparents

The Election Commission of India (ECI) has raised a razor-thin justification to allegations that it has unauthorisedly amended Form 6 to introduce extra-statutory requirements for voters whose names were deleted in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) to return to the electoral rolls.

The wordplay in an ECI affidavit is about an additional declaration form provided alongside Form 6. The declaration form requires deleted voters to provide details of their earlier electoral roll entries or that of their parents or grandparents.

The ECI calls the exercise ‘mapping’. Any perceived mismatch of lack of detail in this regard is broadly termed as ‘logical discrepancy’. In Delhi alone, there were initially 33.12 lakh cases of ‘no-mapping’ or ‘logical discrepancy’.

Petitioners have claimed in court that the additional declaration form was an illegal amendment to Form 6, and has become a tool for exclusion of voters. The ECI cannot have unilaterally altered Form 6. That was the job of the Centre, and not the ECI, they have contended.

The October 26 affidavit, displaying a united face among Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, argues that the petitioners have got it wrong. The affidavit maintained that Form 6 was never changed. The additional declaration form was not a part of the statutory Form 6.

“The additional declaration form is a document provided by SIR orders and is NOT a part of Form 6, which is the statutory Form for inclusion in the electoral roll,” the ECI underscored. The phrase “for inclusion in the electoral roll” used in the ECI affidavit does not fully explain the role of Form 6.

Form 6 is meant exclusively to apply as a fresh voter. Petitioners have challenged this aspect too. They argue that pre-existing electors deleted during the SIR exercise are being forced to apply as fresh voters, compelled to do so under the threat of penal consequences.

ECI said the additional declaration was part of an online push to assist voters. They could file their required details in a single document rather than produce multiple documents for verification like in the Bihar SIR.

On September 26, the ECI had issued a press note that the “declaration attached to Form 6 has been upheld by the Supreme Court. For non-SIR period, the Forms applicable as per Rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used”.

But the Supreme Court had orally clarified on October 12, in open court, that it had neither approved nor disapproved the controversial alterations made to Form 6 in its May 27 judgment in the Bihar SIR challenge.
The oral remark from the Bench had also clearly referred to the additional declaration form as part of the “new Form 6”.

“When the Bihar SIR issue was heard and decided, the new Form 6 was not there. The new Form 6 was neither approved nor disapproved by us. But we will examine it now,” Justice Joymalya Bagchi, who is part of the Bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant, had observed orally.

articles.title: Total voters in Mysuru district down to 22.80 lakh from 27.99 prior to SIR
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The total number of voters in Mysuru district has been put at 22.80 lakh with the publication of the final electoral rolls on Tuesday, marking a reduction of about 5.19 lakh compared to the 27.99 lakh voters on the rolls before the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) began on June 20.

The final electoral rolls of all the eleven Assembly constituencies in Mysuru district is available on the official website of the Chief Electoral Officer of Karnataka https://ceo.karnataka.gov.in/ and Mysuru district’s official website https://mysore.nic.in/ , said a statement by the Deputy Commissioner of Mysuru.
The final electoral rolls of Mysuru district comprise 11,15,225 male voters, 11,64,702 female voters and 140 third-gender voters.

While the draft electoral rolls published on August 24, contained 22,42,452 voters, the addition of 44,648 voters and deletion of 7,033 names resulted in the electorate increasing to 22,80,067 as of October 27.
There has been a net addition of 37,615 voters to the draft electoral rolls, according to the statement.

Notices were issued to 1,28,217 voters in the district who were either not mapped or whose records showed discrepancies. Hearings were conducted in all cases, and 1,26,595 cases had been cleared for final publication, the statement added.

The constituency-wise figures released by the Deputy Commissioner show 1.78 lakh voters in Periyapatna, 1.96 lakh in K.R. Nagar, 2.22 lakh in Hunsur, 1.81 lakh in Chamaraja, 2.04 lakh in H.D. Kote, 1.92 lakh in Nanjangud, 2.88 lakh in Chamundeshwari, 1.81 lakh in Krishnaraja, 2.36 lakh in Narasimharaja, 2.14 lakh in Varuna and 1.82 lakh in T. Narsipur.
A total of 31,313 voters aged 18 and 19 years, including 16,584 males and 14,728 females, figure in the final electoral rolls.
The rolls also comprise 30,458 persons with disabilities, 1,112 service electors, 2,750 VIP electors and 179 NRI electors.

Meanwhile, the statement said the process of continuous updation of electoral rolls is under way. Eligible voters can apply for inclusion or deletion of names and for correction of entries in the electoral rolls.

Form 6 is to be submitted for inclusion of a name in the electoral rolls, Form 7 for deletion of a name, and Form 8 for corrections relating to a voter’s name, relative’s name, relationship details, gender, date of birth, address, photograph, change of address, disability status, mobile number linkage and issue of a duplicate Electoral Photo Identity Card (EPIC).

Meanwhile, the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO) of the Mysuru City Corporation held a meeting with leaders and representatives of political parties in Krishnaraja Assembly constituency to share details of the final electoral rolls published after the SIR exercise.

articles.title: SIR: Over 99.32 lakh names struck off voter list in Karnataka
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Karnataka’s electorate now stands at 4,55,00,011, down from 5,54,32,314 voters before the SIR began

A whopping 99.32 lakh names have been struck off the electoral rolls of Karnataka following the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), with the final list published on Tuesday (October 27). The rolls now include 4,55,00,011 voters, down from 5,54,32,314 before the exercise began.
The constituency-wise electoral rolls can be accessed on the Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) website.

At the draft stage, the electorate had shrunk to 4.46 crore, with over 1.07 crore names deleted. The final roll has seen a net addition of 8.19 lakh names compared with the draft roll. However, the net additions have barely offset the deletions, knocking off nearly a crore from the pre-SIR electorate.

The net addition figures given by the CEO’s office does not indicate how many people who were wrongly excluded have managed to get back on the rolls. Nor does the figure provide a separate break-up of young or first-time voters added during the exercise, making it difficult to ascertain how many of those deleted have been reinstated.

“Karnataka has more than 6.87 crore total population (projected as on the proposed publication year 2026), as per the Population Projections for India and States 2011-2036 published by National Commission on Population Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and 4.54 crore (general electors) in the number of electors in the final roll,” CEO V. Anbu Kumar said, adding that the population-to-electors ratio should ideally be between 60 and 70, and that Karnataka’s ratio stood at 66.11.

However, Mr. Kumar did not explain how the gap of about 2.33 crore between the projected population and the electorate is accounted for, including how much of it comprises people below 18 years, non-voter residents and eligible voters who may have been left out.
ALSO WATCH How did 37 people declare themselves dead in Karnataka’s voter rolls?

The final electorate comprises over 2.25 crore male voters, 2.29 crore female voters and 2,841 third-gender voters. It includes over 6.83 lakh young voters aged 18-19 and more than 3.92 lakh voters aged above 85, besides 44,322 service electors.
The largest pool of electors, 1,02,57,680, belongs to the 30-39 age group, followed by 94,17,853 voters aged between 40 and 49.

Those who applied for inclusion through Form 6 within the claims and objections period, which ended on September 23, will have their names included in the final roll if their applications are accepted. Those who applied after the deadline will be included in supplementary lists, which will be published every quarter after the SIR.

Between June 16 and September 23, the last date for claims and objections, over 7.87 lakh Form 6 applications were received. Of these, 76,231 were rejected and 3,193 remained pending, while 7.08 lakh were accepted, as The Hindu previously reported. The CEO’s office said that over one lakh Form 6 applications submitted after the claims period were also processed to ensure maximum additions.

Till October 26, a total of 10.62 lakh Form 6 applications had been received (since June 16), of which 83,806 were rejected on grounds including applicants having applied unknowingly though already registered elsewhere, failure to submit documents and other reasons. The CEO’s office said instructions had been issued to all District Electoral Officers (DEOs) to reach out to applicants whose applications were rejected and include their names if they could be contacted and found eligible.

articles.title: Keralam Assembly: Govt. has put in place measures to address concerns of expatriates in Saudi, says CM
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Satheesan says the government and NORKA were continuously interacting with various associations of expatriates as well as the Indian embassy and consulate in Saudi Arabia

The State government has put in place a series of measures to address the concerns of expatriate Malayalis in Saudi Arabia amid escalating tensions in West Asia, Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan said in the Keralam Assembly on Tuesday.

Replying to a submission by T.V. Ibrahim, MLA, on the concerning situation in West Asia and the issues of expatriates in Saudi Arabia, the Chief Minister said that any individual cases can be addressed and that the government and NORKA were continuously interacting with various associations of expatriates as well as the Indian embassy and consulate in Saudi Arabia.

He said that complaints received by elected representatives could be forwarded to NORKA for prompt action. A NORKA help desk was opened in Saudi Arabia on October 10 to provide emergency assistance and information to Malayali expatriates and their families. The facility aims to address their concerns, collect details of those requiring urgent assistance and coordinate with the relevant authorities to ensure necessary support.

NORKA Roots has also activated helpline facilities through its Global Contact Centre to provide expatriates with emergency assistance, travel-related information and guidance on the prevailing situation.

The Indian Embassy in Riyadh and the Consulate General of India in Jeddah have established 24-hour control rooms, with their contact numbers made public. Expatriates have been advised to follow the official websites and social media pages of these missions for the latest updates on flight operations, travel disruptions and emergency assistance.

As part of its outreach, NORKA held an online meeting with Malayali expatriates and community organisations in Saudi Arabia on October 24 to assess the situation and identify their concerns. The government is also in touch with expatriate organisations in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries to identify issues requiring urgent intervention and coordinate assistance.

Mr. Satheesan said that the Saudi Arabia government had already announced that visitors holding visit, tourist, Umrah and business visas who were stranded in the country because of flight disruptions could leave without paying fines. He said the intervention of the Keralam government had also contributed to securing this relief.

Arrangements had been made to explore return journeys through airports in neighbouring countries, including Qatar and Bahrain, subject to visa requirements, travel regulations and flight availability. The State government’s representatives in New Delhi were in continuous contact with the Union Ministry of External Affairs, the Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia and the Consulate General in Jeddah to address emerging concerns.

articles.title: Coal India H1 capital expenditure surges 27% to ₹7,966-cr, exceeds target
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: The capex spend in the first half of the fiscal year surpassing the stipulated target of ₹7,286 crore for the period.

State-owned Coal India Ltd (CIL) increased its capital expenditure by 27% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹7,966 crore in the first half of the current financial year, exceeding its stipulated target of ₹7,286 crore for the period.

The miner has utilised more than 48% of its annual capital expenditure outlay of ₹16,500 crore, reflecting a strong investment push towards strengthening mining infrastructure, expanding operational capacity and improving coal evacuation.
Mine infrastructure development, land acquisition, plant and machinery, and diversification together accounted for 79% of the expenditure during the April-September period.

“These strategic investments are expected to strengthen the company’s operational capabilities and support the achievement of its production and supply targets for the ongoing financial year,” Coal India said.

Mine infrastructure development accounted for the largest share of capital expenditure at ₹2,152 crore. The investments were directed primarily towards strengthening coal evacuation and handling infrastructure, including railway sidings and corridors, coal handling plants (CHPs), silos and weighbridges.

Land acquisition was the second-largest expenditure head, accounting for ₹2,033 crore during the first half. The company also spent more than ₹1,000 crore on mine development to facilitate the expansion and operational readiness of mining projects.

The Kolkata-headquartered miner invested ₹1,394 crore in plant and machinery (P&M), including ₹452 crore towards the purchase of heavy earth-moving machinery (HEMM). The remaining expenditure was incurred on washeries and other plant and machinery.

With nearly half of its annual capital expenditure already deployed, Coal India’s investment programme is focused on augmenting mining capacity and addressing potential infrastructure bottlenecks that can constrain production and coal movement. The emphasis on evacuation infrastructure is particularly significant as the company seeks to align its production and supply targets with the capacity to transport coal efficiently.

articles.title: Nayara Energy hikes petrol by ₹5, diesel by ₹3
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: Nayara, which operates 7,108 petrol pumps across the country, raised petrol and diesel prices with effect from early hours of Saturday, October 3, sources said

Nayara Energy, India's largest private fuel retailer, has raised petrol prices by ₹5 per litre and diesel by ₹3 with immediate effect, seeking to narrow the gap between retail prices and rising international oil and refined-product costs, people familiar with the matter said.

The latest increase comes amid renewed pressure on fuel retailers from higher global energy prices and follows a series of price adjustments by Nayara this year as refiners grapple with the impact of geopolitical disruptions on crude and product markets.
Nayara, which operates 7,108 petrol pumps across the country, raised petrol and diesel prices with effect from early hours of Saturday (October 3, 2026), sources said.

Nayara was the first fuel retailer to pass on the surge in international oil prices to consumers when the Iran conflict disrupted energy supplies earlier this year. On March 26, it raised petrol prices by ₹5 a litre and diesel by ₹3, taking the rates at its outlets to ₹100.71 and ₹91.31 a litre, respectively, at the time.
State-owned fuel retailers subsequently began raising pump prices in May.

They increased petrol and diesel prices in a series of staggered moves, with the cumulative increase reaching about ₹7.50 a litre each by late May. The fourth increase on May 25 was ₹2.61 a litre for petrol and ₹2.71 for diesel.

Nayara later reversed its March increase. On July 1, the company cut petrol prices by ₹5 a litre and diesel by ₹3, after international crude prices eased as tensions in West Asia subsided. articles.title: What the new E100 vehicle rules mean | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: The amendments modify Rule 115, which deals with emission standards and related requirements for motor vehicles, and Rule 115E, which contains additional provisions relating to emission testing

The story so far: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has amended the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 , to permit the use of ethanol-based fuels containing up to 100% ethanol (E100) in vehicles. The move paves the way for flex-fuel vehicles, which can run on petrol, ethanol blends of varying proportions, or pure ethanol.
The amendments modify Rule 115, which deals with emission standards and related requirements for motor vehicles, and Rule 115E, which contains additional provisions relating to emission testing.

One of the key changes is the inclusion of E100, or fuel comprising 100% ethanol, alongside E85 in several tables under Rule 115. E85 is a fuel containing up to 85% ethanol, while E100 consists entirely of ethanol, subject to applicable fuel specifications.
The amendments include an explanatory note stating that E85 or E100 may be used only in flex-fuel vehicles designed by original equipment manufacturers.

No. In a press statement, the Ministry sought to allay concerns among motorists, clarifying that a vehicle’s compatibility with E10 or E20 does not establish its suitability for E85. The notification does not require owners of existing vehicles to switch to E85 or modify their vehicles, either now or in the future.

Motorists should check the fuel-compatibility sticker on their vehicle and follow the manufacturer’s guidance in the owner’s manual when choosing fuel at a filling station, the Ministry statement added.

The amendments are expected to facilitate homologation, the official certification process through which authorised agencies, such as the Automotive Research Association of India, verify that vehicles and components comply with technical, safety and environmental standards before they can be approved for sale or use on public roads.
This will help secure type approvals for E100-powered vehicles, supporting their rollout and wider consumer adoption.
Corrections have also been incorporated into fuel classifications, including a reference to gasoline blended with 20% ethanol, or E20, in place of an earlier notation referring to E10.

India achieved its 20% ethanol-blending (E20) target in 2025 , five years ahead of the original 2030 deadline set under the National Policy on Biofuels, 2018. From April 2026, all Bharat Stage-VI (BS-VI) vehicles are required to fully meet E20 emission standards, and all petrol sold across India is mandated to contain 20% ethanol (E20). The policy focus is now widening beyond E20: the government has enabled the regulatory pathway for E85 and E100 vehicles, though these fuels will require compatible flex-fuel vehicles and dedicated dispensing infrastructure.

The main concern is vehicle compatibility. Owners of older or non-E20-compliant vehicles question whether E20 could damage components, raise maintenance costs, or leave them without access to lower-ethanol petrol.

Consumers also question E20’s effect on fuel economy. Ethanol has a lower energy density than petrol; while the government estimates a 5% decline in mileage, some consumers say the loss is greater. Dealers, meanwhile, warn that ethanol’s affinity for water could raise contamination risks during the monsoon, strengthening the case for separate storage and dispensing systems for higher blends. These concerns have prompted calls for a transparent assessment.

articles.title: India poised to refine for world as global capacity declines: Union Minister Hardeep Puri
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: India's refining capacity is currently around 290 million tonnes per annum and is expected to expand further, he said

India is poised to strengthen its position as a global refining hub, with its oil processing capacity set to rise to 300 million tonnes annually by 2030 even as Europe and other parts of the Western world see refinery capacity decline, Union Minister Hardeep Singh Puri said on Tuesday (October 27, 2026).

India's refining capacity is currently around 290 million tonnes per annum and is expected to expand further by scaling up existing facilities and adding new projects, the Union Petroleum Minister said at a news conference on the sidelines of the 29th Energy Technology and Innovation Meet in south Goa.

He said the expansion will allow India not only to meet its domestic energy requirements but also to supply more petroleum products to international markets. "With refining capacity increasing in a big way, we will be in the happy situation of not only refining for ourselves, but for the world," Mr. Puri added.

He contrasted India's expanding refining infrastructure with the decline in global capacity, particularly in Europe, where he estimated that at least 2,50,000 barrels per day of refining capacity was being lost annually.

"Others are going down. Ours is going up," the minister said, pointing to the expansion of Indian refineries at a time when smaller and less efficient facilities in other markets are struggling with logistical costs and operational inefficiencies.
Mr. Puri said India's refining capacity would reach 300 million tonnes per annum by 2030, though the projection may not include all new greenfield refineries in the pipeline.

He said several existing refineries are expanding capacity, with facilities of three million tonnes per annum scaling up to six million tonnes and those with six million tonnes expanding to nine million tonnes.
The Minister also cited the expansion plans of individual refiners to underline India's ability to increase supplies of petroleum products, including diesel, to both domestic and overseas markets.

Responding to questions on whether India would need to restrict exports to ensure domestic availability, Mr. Puri said the country's expanding production capacity would enable it to cater to both markets. "We are in a position to supply more to domestic and more to outside," he said.

Mr. Puri said Indian refiners had been planning capacity and production increases even when domestic diesel consumption growth was subdued, allowing the industry to prepare for higher output as demand patterns evolve.
He also pointed to the absence of new greenfield refineries in the Western world in recent decades, contrasting it with India's continued investments in refining infrastructure.

The Minister said the government's policy direction and the expansion of India's energy sector would further strengthen the country's position in global markets. "Beyond conventional petroleum products, initiatives such as Samudra Manthan and GOBARdhan (Galvanising Organic Bio-Agro Resources Dhan) are also expected to gain momentum, he said, adding that these developments would complement the country's expanding energy infrastructure.

articles.title: IndusInd Bank posts profit of ₹1,242 crores in Q2; asset quality improvement and interest income drives growth
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: The bank’s bottom line for Q2FY27 was supported by a rise in net interest income, which stood at ₹4,569 crore as against ₹4,409 crores a year ago

IndusInd Bank Limited posted a net profit of ₹1,242 crore for the quarter ended September, up 20% sequentially and trimming net loss of ₹437 for the same quarter in the preceding year. The bank had incurred net loss for the same period in previous year due to an increase in microfinance provisioning and write-offs.

The bank’s bottom line for Q2FY27 was supported by a rise in net interest income, which stood at ₹4,569 crore as against ₹4,409 crores a year ago. Sequentially, interest income declined by 2%. NII for half year (H1FY27) rose to ₹9,254, up 2.3% on year.

Asset quality of the bank improved substantially, with gross non-performing assets (NPA) ratio at 2.73% compared to 3.60% on year and net NPA declining to 0.83% from 1.04% in Q2FY26. However, the net interest margin of the bank slipped to 3.23% from 3.32% a year ago.

Net revenue of the bank for the period rose to ₹6,817 crores compared to ₹6,00 crores a year. A decline in operating expenses also helped push the bottom-line numbers, with expenses slipping to ₹3,943 crores in July-Septemeber from ₹4,013 crore for the same period last year.
Deposits of the bank rose 10% year-on-year to ₹4.28 crores. Advances of the bank for the period stood at 3.63 crores.
IndusInd held provisions of $9,012 crore as of September 30, with the provision coverage ratio at 70%.

IndusInd Bank raised nearly $3.5 billion via the Reserve Bank of India’s special window for foreign currency non-resident bank (FCNR-B) account, which was impacted the contraction in NIM. The bank said recovery in margin related to FCNR-B is expected over the next two quarters.

“Q2 reflects the growing strength of the IndusInd Bank franchise and the progress we have made in rebuilding momentum across the business. Our Q2 results demonstrate that the growth has strengthened, profitability has improved, asset quality trends remain encouraging, and our funding profile is becoming more granular and resilient,” Rajiv Anand, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of IndusInd Bank said.

The bank also informed the exchanges on Friday (October 23, 2026) that the Board of Directors of the lender has appointed Priyanka Sinha as an Additional Director in the category of Non-Executive Independent Director for a period of four consecutive years, till October 22, 2030.

Speaking to the media at post-earnings conference call, the bank said it remains confident of reaching a 1% exit return on assets for FY27. Bank also expects loans growth momentum to continue driven by retail and wholesale lending. Shares of IndusInd Bank Ltd closed at ₹835.00 on Friday, down 1.76%, on the BSE.

articles.title: BPCL shifts crude sourcing towards Middle East as Russian oil loses price edge
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: Russian crude accounted for 37% of their import basket in the second quarter.

Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL) tapped more into Middle Eastern crude as Russian oil lost its price advantage and also due to rising freight costs, with the shift becoming more pronounced in November, Vetsa Ramakrishna Gupta, Director (Finance), told analysts during a post-results call on Monday.

“Our spot crude share remained at around 67% in the second quarter, while Russian grade accounted for approximately 37% of our total crude procurement, both broadly in line with the previous quarter,” Mr. Gupta said, adding that the company increased purchases from the Middle East as supplies from the region improved.

Russia accounted for 37% of BPCL’s crude basket in the September quarter, followed by Saudi Arabia at 19%, Abu Dhabi at 17%, the U.S. at 9% and Oman at 6%. The remaining supplies came from countries contributing 1-4% each.
As of September-end, BPCL held about 22 days of crude inventory, with sourcing requirements tied up through December.
Mr. Gupta said the share of Russian crude in October was expected to remain “more or less the same”, although procurement volumes would be lower for November.

“October, our requirement from Russia slightly came down but in the month of November, the cargoes from Russia significantly reduced due to [reduced] commercial viability [compared to that from Middle East], mainly the increase in the freight,” he said, adding that the company did not receive attractive offers for Russian crude in November.

Russian crude was available at a premium of $12-$13 per barrel over benchmark prices in October. The premium has narrowed to $1-$2 per barrel for December cargoes, Mr. Gupta said, although freight costs remain high.
“Maybe today, Russian cargo is preferable than a Middle Eastern cargo for December month because November [procurement] we have already concluded,” he said.

BPCL also diversified its liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) sourcing during the quarter. Supplies from the Arab Gulf improved, while the US accounted for about 48% of LPG imports in the September quarter.
Softening Saudi Contract Prices (Saudi CP), the benchmark for LPG pricing, helped reduce under-recoveries to an average ₹290 per cylinder in the September quarter from ₹507 in the June quarter.

Under-recoveries are expected to be ₹245 per cylinder in October and are expected to rise to ₹328 in November, Mr. Gupta said. BPCL currently holds 32 days of LPG inventory, including supplies in transit.
The company has also diversified liquefied natural gas (LNG) procurement by increasing spot purchases from the US, Oman and West Africa.

articles.title: Egypt detains prominent journalist Lina Attalah after trial
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Egyptian security forces detained prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, the chief editor of leading independent news website Mada Masr , after her trial hearing on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), her outlet reported.

A court fined Ms. Attalah three million Egyptian pounds (around $53,400) for operating the website without a licence, the maximum possible penalty for the misdemeanour she was charged with, and ordered Mada's closure.

"Security personnel then surrounded Attalah, lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom, where she remains in custody in the courthouse," said the independent media, which says it has not received a response from authorities about its licence application since 2023.
Her trial marks what rights groups have described as a sharp escalation in Cairo's crackdown on press freedom.
It comes weeks after the high-profile arrest of an entire fact-checking newsroom, on charges of fake news, which are frequently levelled against media seen to be critical of the government.
Hossam Bahgat, head of prominent rights group the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), was present at the court and gave AFP an account of events.

After a brief recess during the hearing Tuesday (October 27), the defence team said the judge ordered the room cleared except for Ms. Attalah and her lawyers, before security officers also entered the room.
Ms. Attalah's eight-person defence team had made procedural requests denied by the court, which then announced it had appointed its own lawyer for the journalist.

"In a move that astonished all those present, the judge recorded in the official court minutes that the court had appointed a lawyer from the Lawyers' Syndicate to represent the defence," Mr. Bahgat said.

"Lina herself spoke up to object to this lawyer being appointed to represent her, which the judge refused to record in the court minutes. In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer -- who had not uttered a single word -- and entered them into the official record," he added.

The judge then announced the three million Egyptian pound fine and ordered Mada's closure "amid shouts and protests from the defence", before Ms. Attalah was detained by the security personnel in the room.
Her defence team is currently trying to secure her release on bail.

articles.title: Syria condemns deadly Jordan strikes as ‘unacceptable violation’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: In the worst crisis between the neighbours since the ouster of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, Jordan said it had great respect for Syria and expressed regret for civilian casualties
Syria on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) condemned deadly strikes on the country's south a day earlier that Jordan said killed more than 20 jihadists as retaliation for a gun attack on a church.

In the worst crisis between the neighbours since the ouster of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, Jordan said it had "great respect" for Syria and expressed regret for civilian casualties.

Its Monday (October 26) night strikes came after gunmen last week killed nine people and wounded 25 others during a funeral service at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in southern Jordan's Karak governorate, an attack that sparked shock across the country.
While Jordan has insisted it coordinated its airstrikes with Syria, Damascus has denied the claim and the two sides have provided differing tolls.
Syria's civil defence agency said the Jordanian strikes killed seven people including three children.

Jordan's government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani said that "the preliminary results... indicate significant losses among Daesh's ranks -- estimated at more than 20 fighters", using an Arabic acronym for the Islamic State jihadist group.
He also said "a large weapons depot belonging to the organisation" had been destroyed.
Mr. Momani expressed regret for any civilian casualties, saying Jordan had avoided targeting locations where it believed civilians were present.
Syria's Foreign Ministry issued a "condemnation and rejection" of the strikes, calling them "an unacceptable violation and breach of Syrian airspace without any prior coordination".
It also said the raid was "a blatant violation of the principles of good-neighbourliness and Syrian national sovereignty".
Amman appeared keen to put an end to the crisis, with Mr. Momani saying that "Jordan holds great respect for the Syrian state and its brotherly people".
Syria said five people including a woman and three children were killed in the village of Al-Taf in Daraa province, which borders Jordan, with two other people killed elsewhere in the south.

articles.title: Lula’s win gives Brazil an opportunity to cement its climate leadership, but challenges remain
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: On a global level, Brazil has come to play a major role in climate negotiations because of its simultaneous status as a major oil producer and, especially under Lula, a strong advocate of international climate cooperation

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva winning his fourth term as Brazil’s President has also interrupted a series of right-wing electoral wins in Latin America. That said, Brazil and Mexico are now the sole left-wing governments among the region’s largest economies. And while it would be reductive to believe the left is more welcoming of climate action and the right is more disdainful, Mr. Lula also faces significant challenges in his role on the issue both in Brazil and beyond.

His foremost opportunity will be to have Brazil cement its mantle of leadership. Brazil is somewhat unique: it is Latin America’s largest economy, the world’s fifth-largest by area, host to most of the Amazon and, crucially, has diplomatic relationships with the European Union, the U.S., China, the BRICS countries, and many other developing economies — potentially allowing Mr. Lula to negotiate across the divides that currently frustrate climate agreements. In fact, China has made tariffs on clean energy technologies a priority for the COP31 summit, set to commence in under a fortnight in Türkiye, with Beijing arguing against protectionist trade measures while the EU and the U.S. have raised concerns about dependence on Chinese manufacturers.

On the regional level, Brazil straddles several problems, including deforestation in the Amazon, illegal mining, forest fires, and a degrading river basin, that demand region-wide cooperation, including the representation of Indigenous groups. Mr. Lula revived such cooperation to a commendable degree through the Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organisation (ACTO), by hosting the Belém summit in 2023, and by making further commitments at the Bogotá summit in 2025.

However, the optimism Mr. Lula warrants is tempered by the Belém Declaration in 2023 failing to establish a binding collective deadline to end deforestation in the Amazon rainforest and to prohibit the development of new oil projects in the region. Both the dependence of the Amazonian countries on agriculture, petroleum, and mining and the powers and resources available to their regulators are markedly different, and political changes are not conducive to sustaining regional cooperation.

Mr. Lula’s fourth term could thus keep ACTO going, especially on cross-border enforcement and in preserving a forum for governments to negotiate on conflicting political priorities. But given the divergent economic incentives and weak national institutions, lasting change means ACTO also developing common monitoring and financing arrangements.

On a more global level, Brazil has come to play a major role in climate negotiations because of its simultaneous status as a major oil producer and, especially under Lula, a strong advocate of international climate cooperation.

In fact, the day after Mr. Lula’s election win, the Netherlands announced that it intends to contribute up to $500 million over a decade, on certain conditions, to Brazil’s ‘Tropical Forest Forever Facility’ (TFFF). The pledge brings the sum of commitments announced thus far to $7.8 billion, against the target of $10 billion by the end of 2026. Lula’s continuing government will help establish the TFFF in its formative years and steady its hand as a potentially new international financial institution.

In the same spirit, Colombia and the Netherlands convened the first international conference dedicated to transitioning away from fossil fuels in April. Fifty-seven countries, including Brazil, participated to develop proposals for financial cooperation, among other matters, and planned for a second meeting in 2027.

As well, at the COP30 climate talks that Brazil presided over last year, Mr. Lula supported proposals to develop an international roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, drawing support from more than 80 countries, but the summit could not see through due to opposition from Russia and Saudi Arabia, among others. The April conference has thus emerged as a parallel mechanism to effect action.

Yet another avenue in the same vein is the EU-Mercosur relationship. The EU and the South American trade bloc signed their interim trade and partnership agreements in January. The latter’s ratification will be significant because they require governments to comply with the Paris Agreement — and could allow Mr. Lula’s climate diplomacy to work through UN negotiations as well as trade and investment relationships to create longer-lasting economic commitments. On the flip side, it may also create greater incentives to convert forestland for other use, so Lula and his peers will have to institute more effective protections.

All this said, while preserving cooperation is essential to effective climate action, it will amount to little if it does not also cut emissions. In fact, continuity in international climate diplomacy could prevent regression without also yielding the acceleration required to meet climate goals. The UN Environment Programme has already found that even if all countries deliver on their pledges vis-à-vis the Paris Agreement, the world is on course to warming by 2.6°C by the end of the century.

Brazil’s incoming conservative Congress is also likely to constrain the Lula government’s ability to sustain expenditure — even if his term provides continuity through 2030, an important year that numerous climate-related commitments use as a deadline or milestone year. That Mr. Lula’s win is a record also raises the prospect of policy whiplash, especially against programmes that depend on his personal political authority, when his last term ends.

On the flip side, it may also create greater incentives to convert forestland for other use, so Lula and his peers will have to institute more effective protections.

All this said, while preserving cooperation is essential to effective climate action, it will amount to little if it does not also cut emissions. In fact, continuity in international climate diplomacy could prevent regression without also yielding the acceleration required to meet climate goals. The UN Environment Programme has already found that even if all countries deliver on their pledges vis-à-vis the Paris Agreement, the world is on course to warming by 2.6°C by the end of the century.

Brazil’s incoming conservative Congress is also likely to constrain the Lula government’s ability to sustain expenditure — even if his term provides continuity through 2030, an important year that numerous climate-related commitments use as a deadline or milestone year. That Mr. Lula’s win is a record also raises the prospect of policy whiplash, especially against programmes that depend on his personal political authority, when his last term ends.

3. That Mr. Lula’s win is a record also raises the prospect of policy whiplash, especially against programmes that depend on his personal political authority, when his last term ends.

articles.title: Israel holds polls amid uncertainty over Netanyahu’s future, coalition numbers
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Opposition leaders Gadi Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett are challenging PM Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition, with opinion polls showing neither bloc assured of the 61 seats needed for a majority

Israel is holding parliamentary elections on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seeking to retain power amid debate over the government’s handling of the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023, the subsequent wars, and its domestic and foreign policies.

The election is widely seen as a test of Mr. Netanyahu’s leadership, as Opposition leaders, including former military chief Gadi Eisenkot and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, seek to challenge his right-wing coalition. Opinion polls indicate neither bloc is assured of the parliamentary majority needed to form a government.
A graphic showing the party-wise split of the outgoing Knesset in Israel

Israel, roughly the size of north-eastern India’s Mizoram State, uses a nationwide proportional representation system, with the entire country serving as a single electoral constituency to elect the 120 members of the Knesset, Israel’s parliament.

Voters do not elect individual members of parliament; instead, they vote for closed party lists, a system that allows numerous political parties to compete for seats. To enter the Knesset, a party must cross the 3.25% electoral threshold, a requirement that often prompts pre-election alliances and mergers.

The Knesset serves a four-year term, but elections can be held early if it votes to dissolve itself, fails to approve the State budget within the prescribed period, or a new government cannot be formed.

The party winning the most seats does not automatically form the government; after the election, the President consults political factions and appoints a lawmaker to form a government, who must secure the support of at least 61 lawmakers.
A graphic showing key candidates, figures and steps in Israel’s election for Prime Minister

Mr. Netanyahu, leader of the right-wing Likud party, has served as Israel’s Prime Minister for nearly 19 years across three separate periods since 1996. He seeks to retain power after a period marked by the October 7 attack, which took place three years ago, and the multiple military campaigns that followed.

The Hamas-led assault of 2023 killed about 1,200 people in Israel and triggered the war in Gaza, which subsequently widened into a broader regional conflict involving Israel, Iran and other armed groups.

Following the attack, Israel launched a large-scale military campaign in the Gaza Strip, involving airstrikes, ground operations and restrictions that severely disrupted civilian life. According to Gaza’s health ministry, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been reported killed and over 175,000 injured since the start of the war.

Security and accountability for the October 7, 2023, attack are central issues in the campaign. Mr. Netanyahu also faces charges of fraud, breach of trust and bribery, which he denies. The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for him in 2024, over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.

articles.title: ‘Cruel’ jail conditions caused dozens of Nigerian miners to suffocate: probe
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Screams for help and banging the door yielded no response from guards on duty, according to survivors

Poor jail conditions led to the deaths of more than 30 miners arrested on suspicion of illegal gold mining in central Nigeria last month, investigators said Tuesday, describing their treatment as "cruel and inhuman".

Thirty-three young men were found dead after they were thrown inside a crowded cell in Minna, the capital of central Niger state, in September after their arrest by the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) , a paramilitary government agency.
Survivors recounted being crammed in the cell with poor ventilation and some said a substance that stung their throats and noses was sprayed into the cell before the door was slammed shut.
Screams for help and banging the door yielded no response from guards on duty, according to survivors.

Medical and forensic evidence showed the deaths resulted from "environmental asphyxia, acute respiratory failure caused by prolonged confinement in a severely overcrowded and poorly ventilated detention cell aggravated by heat stress and dehydration", the head of the investigating team, Jonathan Kure, said while presenting the report to the government.
"The committee concluded that these circumstances amounted to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment," he said.
Niger state authorities initially put the death toll at 37, but the investigating committee said it had established 33 deaths.

"The committee confirmed 33 as the verified casualty figure because higher numbers reported immediately after the incident could not be reconciled with available records and identified victims," said Kure, adding that 14 of the dead were minors.

articles.title: India must make its defence chips end-to-end, say scientists
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: At The Hindu Semiconductor Summit, V.K. Saraswat, A. Sivathanu Pillai and Deleep Nair warn that imported chips leave network-centric weapons vulnerable, and that waiting until 2030-35 for advanced nodes would be too late

India’s increasingly network-centric weapons, from the BrahMos cruise missile to the proposed Sudarshan Chakra air defence shield, will remain vulnerable so long as the semiconductors inside them are imported, senior defence scientists said on Tuesday, calling for chips to be designed, manufactured and packaged end-to-end in the country.

Speaking at the ‘Chips for the Next Battlefield: Semiconductors, AI & the Future of Defense’ panel at SRM Presents The Hindu Semiconductor Summit 2026 here, former Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) Director General V.K. Saraswat said warfare had moved from platform-centric fighting to network-centric operations, in which command, control and communications riding on semiconductors decide the outcome.

“What you saw in Operation Sindoor … is that we are today more or less equipped with complete network-centric capability,” Dr. Saraswat said. Sudarshan Chakra, the multi-layer, multi-domain air defence system announced by the Prime Minister, would fuse data from satellite, sea, air and land-based sensors using artificial intelligence-enabled software, he added. “But we have realised that is not enough for future warfare, for long-duration warfare, to take care of saturation attacks.” Drone swarms, he noted, now arrive “in hundreds and thousands”, and directed energy weapons were needed alongside ballistic missile defence.

A. Sivathanu Pillai, founder, CEO and Managing Director of BrahMos Aerospace, said precision was the point at which chips entered the picture. A BrahMos missile given a target’s coordinates changes course within milliseconds to secure a “bullseye hit”, he said. “How has the intelligence come to that? It is a processor and the software. So semiconductors play a very important role there.” He added that the Light Combat Aircraft Mark 2 could, on a single mission, process as much data as the entire MiG-21 fleet processed in 1971, and that even Chandrayaan-3’s landing was achieved with semiconductor systems that “was all imported, you know; that was our problem”.

Most Indian defence systems are based on 28-nanometre chips, Dr. Pillai said, while the world has moved to 3 nanometres. India is compensating for weaker hardware with software — for instance, by collating data from multiple GPS sources because it does not have a military satellite giving it military-specification accuracy, but that approach would not be enough for hypersonic systems, he argued.

“The government has said that 3 nanometre we will achieve sometime around 2030 to 35. That is too late in the present situation,” Dr. Pillai said, warning that controls on materials, devices and chip-making equipment were coming. “If you want to wait for 2030 to 35 to achieve it, you will miss the bus.” The equipment needed to make a foundry, and not just the foundry itself, would also have to be produced in India, he said.

Dr. Saraswat added that advanced nodes of 5, 3 and 2 nanometres would be essential for AI systems, including large language models and AI at the edge, even if 28-nanometre chips, and perhaps 14-nanometre chips, could carry today’s Sudarshan Chakra requirements.

Deleep Nair, Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Madras, traced how far behind domestic fabrication remains. India received complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology from the Radio Corporation of America before Taiwan did, he said, but the Semiconductor Complex Limited (SCL) in Chandigarh was shut for a long period after a fire in the late 1980s. The leading-edge technology running in India today, at SCL, is 180 nanometres, he said, which is the same that Intel, AMD and IBM had in the mid-1990s. Under the DRDO, the Gallium Arsenide Enabling Technology Centre (GAETEC) works on gallium arsenide and gallium nitride, he added.

That dependence carries a security risk, Dr. Saraswat said, recalling how supplies of the 8086/8087 processors used in the first Prithvi missile were curtailed once the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme was announced, and dried up further under the Missile Technology Control Regime. “These devices, if they are compromised while they are being manufactured, then your weapon is compromised,” he said, citing Stuxnet, in which a flaw introduced during fabrication allowed a controller running centrifuges at an Iranian enrichment plant to be remotely overrun. Communication links, foreign cloud infrastructure and foreign GPS-based position, navigation and timing systems posed the same problem, he said: “If the cloud is sitting outside, the entire information going through my network-centric warfare system through the cloud, I am compromised.”

The prescription from the panel was end-to-end domestic capability under the India Semiconductor Mission covering materials, design, manufacturing, equipment and human resources, including compound semiconductors such as gallium nitride and silicon carbide, which sit at the front end of radars and imaging systems. The waiting line for extreme ultraviolet lithography equipment needed for advanced nodes was already four to five years, Dr. Saraswat noted.

Both he and Dr. Pillai called for research and development fabs in the IITs and other universities, on the model of Belgium’s Interuniversity Microelectronics Centre, warning that without them India would again have to import technology for the next generation, such as neuromorphic chips. Dr. Pillai said India already accounted for 20% of the world’s chip design capability. “Why not go in a big way to develop the manpower? Instead of 20%, let us take 50% of the design we should do for the world,” he said, adding that universities should also take up packaging and testing.

Dr. Nair said the Tata fab in Gujarat, being set up with a technology licence from Taiwan’s Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation, would bring the 40-nanometre node, on which a lot of applications could run, while packaging plants were coming up under the mission.
