🚀 Science, Tech & Environment 📅 27 Oct 2026 • IN-APP NEWSPAPER PRINT EDITION

India must make its defence chips end-to-end, say scientists

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports

At The Hindu Semiconductor Summit, V.K. Saraswat, A. Sivathanu Pillai and Deleep Nair warn that imported chips leave network-centric weapons vulnerable, and that waiting until 2030-35 for advanced nodes would be too late

India’s increasingly network-centric weapons, from the BrahMos cruise missile to the proposed Sudarshan Chakra air defence shield, will remain vulnerable so long as the semiconductors inside them are imported, senior defence scientists said on Tuesday, calling for chips to be designed, manufactured and packaged end-to-end in the country.

Speaking at the ‘Chips for the Next Battlefield: Semiconductors, AI & the Future of Defense’ panel at SRM Presents The Hindu Semiconductor Summit 2026 here, former Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) Director General V.K. Saraswat said warfare had moved from platform-centric fighting to network-centric operations, in which command, control and communications riding on semiconductors decide the outcome.

“What you saw in Operation Sindoor … is that we are today more or less equipped with complete network-centric capability,” Dr. Saraswat said. Sudarshan Chakra, the multi-layer, multi-domain air defence system announced by the Prime Minister, would fuse data from satellite, sea, air and land-based sensors using artificial intelligence-enabled software, he added. “But we have realised that is not enough for future warfare, for long-duration warfare, to take care of saturation attacks.” Drone swarms, he noted, now arrive “in hundreds and thousands”, and directed energy weapons were needed alongside ballistic missile defence.

A. Sivathanu Pillai, founder, CEO and Managing Director of BrahMos Aerospace, said precision was the point at which chips entered the picture. A BrahMos missile given a target’s coordinates changes course within milliseconds to secure a “bullseye hit”, he said. “How has the intelligence come to that? It is a processor and the software. So semiconductors play a very important role there.” He added that the Light Combat Aircraft Mark 2 could, on a single mission, process as much data as the entire MiG-21 fleet processed in 1971, and that even Chandrayaan-3’s landing was achieved with semiconductor systems that “was all imported, you know; that was our problem”.

Most Indian defence systems are based on 28-nanometre chips, Dr. Pillai said, while the world has moved to 3 nanometres. India is compensating for weaker hardware with software — for instance, by collating data from multiple GPS sources because it does not have a military satellite giving it military-specification accuracy, but that approach would not be enough for hypersonic systems, he argued.

“The government has said that 3 nanometre we will achieve sometime around 2030 to 35. That is too late in the present situation,” Dr. Pillai said, warning that controls on materials, devices and chip-making equipment were coming. “If you want to wait for 2030 to 35 to achieve it, you will miss the bus.” The equipment needed to make a foundry, and not just the foundry itself, would also have to be produced in India, he said.

Dr. Saraswat added that advanced nodes of 5, 3 and 2 nanometres would be essential for AI systems, including large language models and AI at the edge, even if 28-nanometre chips, and perhaps 14-nanometre chips, could carry today’s Sudarshan Chakra requirements.

Deleep Nair, Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Madras, traced how far behind domestic fabrication remains. India received complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology from the Radio Corporation of America before Taiwan did, he said, but the Semiconductor Complex Limited (SCL) in Chandigarh was shut for a long period after a fire in the late 1980s. The leading-edge technology running in India today, at SCL, is 180 nanometres, he said, which is the same that Intel, AMD and IBM had in the mid-1990s. Under the DRDO, the Gallium Arsenide Enabling Technology Centre (GAETEC) works on gallium arsenide and gallium nitride, he added.

That dependence carries a security risk, Dr. Saraswat said, recalling how supplies of the 8086/8087 processors used in the first Prithvi missile were curtailed once the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme was announced, and dried up further under the Missile Technology Control Regime. “These devices, if they are compromised while they are being manufactured, then your weapon is compromised,” he said, citing Stuxnet, in which a flaw introduced during fabrication allowed a controller running centrifuges at an Iranian enrichment plant to be remotely overrun. Communication links, foreign cloud infrastructure and foreign GPS-based position, navigation and timing systems posed the same problem, he said: “If the cloud is sitting outside, the entire information going through my network-centric warfare system through the cloud, I am compromised.”

The prescription from the panel was end-to-end domestic capability under the India Semiconductor Mission covering materials, design, manufacturing, equipment and human resources, including compound semiconductors such as gallium nitride and silicon carbide, which sit at the front end of radars and imaging systems. The waiting line for extreme ultraviolet lithography equipment needed for advanced nodes was already four to five years, Dr. Saraswat noted.

Both he and Dr. Pillai called for research and development fabs in the IITs and other universities, on the model of Belgium’s Interuniversity Microelectronics Centre, warning that without them India would again have to import technology for the next generation, such as neuromorphic chips. Dr. Pillai said India already accounted for 20% of the world’s chip design capability. “Why not go in a big way to develop the manpower? Instead of 20%, let us take 50% of the design we should do for the world,” he said, adding that universities should also take up packaging and testing.

Dr. Nair said the Tata fab in Gujarat, being set up with a technology licence from Taiwan’s Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation, would bring the 40-nanometre node, on which a lot of applications could run, while packaging plants were coming up under the mission.

articles.title: India must build semiconductor capabilities beyond chip design, says DG of Semiconductor Laboratory
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Kamaljeet Singh flags foreign dependence on critical inputs; calls for stronger R&D, manufacturing infrastructure and specialised skills

India needs to strengthen capabilities across the semiconductor value chain, from manufacturing and materials to research and specialised skills, to reduce dependence on foreign technologies and build a resilient domestic ecosystem, Dr. Kamaljeet Singh, Director-General of the Semiconductor Laboratory (SCL), Mohali, said on Tuesday (October 27, 2026).

Speaking at the inaugural session of the Semiconductor Summit 2026, organised by SRM Institute of Science and Technology in association with The Hindu , he said India had a significant presence in semiconductor design but remained dependent on foreign suppliers for critical inputs, including electronic design automation (EDA) tools.
“But the EDA tools which we are using also come from the U.S. So that is why all dependencies are foreign,” he said.

Mr. Singh said the country needed to overcome several challenges to become a technological power. “Technology is one of the challenges, talent is one of the challenges, resources is one of the challenges, time is the challenge, acceptability is the challenge and capital is the challenge,” he said.

He said India needed to build capabilities not only in chip design and fabrication but also in the supporting supply chain, including manufacturing equipment, raw materials, chemicals, gases and packaging materials. Semiconductor supply chains were concentrated in a small number of countries, making access to these inputs critical, he said.
India’s semiconductor requirements were substantial, and the country needed to manufacture more of the chips it used domestically, Mr. Singh said.

He highlighted the need to connect research with manufacturing, arguing that developing semiconductor technologies required researchers, pilot lines, manufacturing facilities and industry participation.
“You need a lot of researchers to come into place, you need a manufacturing unit, you need a lot of technology to be developed to attain the system design and architecture,” he said.

Mr. Singh said the India Semiconductor Mission had supported the development of domestic capabilities. Under the first phase, ₹76,000 crore had been pumped in, with 12 projects approved, five of which had been operationalised and another expected to become operational, he said.

The second phase of the mission had six pillars, including chip design, manufacturing, materials and machinery, with research and development and skill development added as two further areas of focus, he said.
He stressed that India needed to strengthen specialised engineering and manufacturing capabilities alongside its existing design talent.

Mr. Singh highlighted SCL’s efforts to make semiconductor design education more accessible through open-source tools. The laboratory had integrated its process design kit (PDK) with open-source tools so that students unable to afford commercial EDA software could learn chip design.

articles.title: Merck drug extends survival in endometrial cancer trial, wins U.S. priority review
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The drug delivers a cancer-killing payload to cells that carry a protein common in endometrial tumours

The U.S. health regulator has accepted Merck’s experimental targeted drug for a priority review based on data from a late-stage trial where it extended survival in women with an advanced form of endometrial cancer.
The drug, sacituzumab tirumotecan, also known as sac-TMT, delivers a cancer-killing payload to cells that carry a protein called TROP2, which is common in endometrial tumors.

The trial enrolled 776 patients whose cancer had returned or progressed after earlier treatment. Patients were randomly assigned to sac-TMT or to a chemotherapy their doctor chose, either doxorubicin or paclitaxel.
Results showed sac-TMT reduced the risk of death by 32%, with patients living a median of 19 months compared with 12.1 months on standard chemotherapy.
The treatment also reduced the risk of cancer progression or death by 41%, with patients remaining progression-free for a median of 7.2 months compared with 3.9 months on chemotherapy.
In addition, about 35% of sac-TMT patients saw their tumors shrink, compared with 17% on chemotherapy.
A regulatory decision is expected by June 2027, Merck said. The trial data was presented at the ESMO medical congress.

“Based on discussions with the FDA, the company is hopeful for an approval before the PDUFA date to bring sac-TMT to patients as quickly as possible,” said Dean Y. Li, president, Merck Research Laboratories.
Severe treatment-related side effects were more frequent with sac-TMT, affecting about 54% of patients compared with 41% on chemotherapy. About 3% of patients stopped treatment due to side effects.
About 68,000 cases of endometrial cancer are expected to be diagnosed in the United States in 2026, with over 14,000 deaths, according to the American Cancer Society.
Jefferies analysts project peak sales of roughly $900 million in endometrial cancer for the drug and $9 billion across all potential indications.
Merck is developing the drug with Chinese biotech firm Kelun-Biotech, which discovered the therapy.

articles.title: Chip war exposes India’s semiconductor vulnerabilities, industry leaders say
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: U.S.–China tensions underscore need for domestic technology capabilities and resilient supply chains; industry flags gaps in materials, manufacturing expertise and specialised talent

As geopolitical tensions reshape the global semiconductor industry, India needs to develop its own technology capabilities, reduce critical supply-chain dependencies, and build resilience through international partnerships, industry leaders said at a panel discussion on ‘The Chip War: Technology, Geopolitics and India’s Challenges’ at the Semiconductor Summit 2026 in Chennai.

The panellists said India needed to identify areas where it could develop technologies of its own while building domestic manufacturing capabilities and diversifying sources of supply, as countries increasingly seek to secure access to semiconductor technologies, materials and manufacturing capacity.

Sharat Kaul, India representative of the International Electronics Manufacturing Initiative (iNEMI), said the country should not dismiss outsourced semiconductor assembly and testing (OSAT) projects as an inadequate starting point. Semiconductor manufacturing requires specialised equipment, materials, talent and infrastructure, making it necessary to build the ecosystem progressively. “We have to crawl before we walk. We have to walk before we run,” he said.
Mr. Kaul said semiconductor sovereignty did not mean producing everything domestically.

“Sovereignty doesn’t necessarily mean that we do everything ourselves. It means that we build reliance and resilience. A bigger part is really resilience,” he said, citing the importance of maintaining multiple supply-chain options through partnerships with friendly nations.

He also identified advanced packaging, which integrates multiple chips on a single substrate, as an opportunity for India to narrow its technological gap with established semiconductor manufacturing countries.

“The tipping point in the industry is going to be advanced packaging,” he said, pointing to the potential of two-and-a-half-dimensional and three-dimensional technologies amid geopolitical tensions and efforts by countries such as the United States to bring advanced manufacturing within their borders.
Sandeep Garg, chief executive officer and board member of Indichip Semiconductors, said India needed to manufacture semiconductor devices required by its own industries instead of relying on imports.
“The time has come for manufacturing and we have to manufacture our own devices,” he said.

Drawing on his industry experience, Dr. Garg said major semiconductor companies had not established fabrication facilities in India despite being present in the country for decades. India needed to create greater domestic value addition rather than assume its large market alone would attract manufacturing investment, he argued.

Indichip is setting up an integrated device manufacturing facility covering fabrication, assembly and testing, and final modules, with an investment of more than ₹15,000 crore, he said. The company focuses on silicon carbide power devices used in sectors including energy, electric mobility, railways, defence and data centres.
Dr. Garg estimated that India’s silicon carbide market could grow from about ₹13,000 crore in 2030 to ₹1 lakh crore by 2035.

articles.title: ‘India has engineers, but needs more chip-ready ones’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: At The Hindu Semiconductor Summit, industry and government agree the shortage is of industry-ready talent and exposure, and that success should be measured by intellectual property and products, not certificates.

India is not short of engineers, but of engineers who are ready to build chips, panelists said on Tuesday, arguing that the talent gap facing the semiconductor mission is one of practical competence, exposure and experience across the whole value chain, rather than of numbers.

Speaking at the ‘Who Will Build India’s Chips? Bridging the Semiconductor Talent Gap’ panel at SRM Presents The Hindu Semiconductor Summit 2026 here, Ranjith Kumar T.C., Director, PRSsemicon Technologies, said the country had 10,000 to 15,000 engineering colleges and 15 lakh to 20 lakh engineers passing out every year. “The actual shortfall is not the number of graduates that we have. The actual shortfall would be the skilled or the industry ready engineers that we are looking at,” he said, describing the shift needed as one “from knowing to doing,” that is, from learning a concept to bringing out a chip, inculcated during college itself.

Sujhatha, Senior Manager, Guidance, Government of Tamil Nadu, agreed that India was not short of people. articles.title: In the crossfire: on India and the Saudi-Houthi conflict
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: India must adopt a pro-active position in the Saudi-Houthi conflict

The killing of an Indian national in a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport is a grim reminder of the dangers the kingdom’s Indian community faces as the conflict between Riyadh and Yemen’s Shia militants escalates. Since the fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed in July, at least two Indians have been killed and 14 others wounded. On Thursday, the Houthis claimed that a yacht with 14 Indians was targeted by Saudi forces near Yemen’s Zuqar island in the Red Sea and that rescue operations were under way. As the Houthis, who control parts of Northern Yemen and its entire Red Sea coast, step up attacks on Saudi infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports, Indians, who are the kingdom’s largest expat community, risk getting caught in the crossfire. With flights disrupted, thousands of Indian pilgrims are stranded. India has condemned Houthi attacks, saying that it “stands in solidarity” with Saudi Arabia. With no end in sight to the fighting and a high possibility of Israel and the U.S. resuming their Iran strikes, further violence and instability in West Asia could make India’s choices increasingly difficult.

The Saudi-Houthi conflict dates back to the Houthi takeover of Sana’a, Yemen’s capital, in 2014. A year later, Saudi Arabia began bombing Yemen to drive the Houthis out. But years of Saudi bombing of one of the poorest Arab countries have proved counterproductive; the Houthis consolidated support among the tribes of northern Yemen and built a powerful territorial army and naval force. The Saudi-Houthi ceasefire of 2022 collapsed in July 2026 after Saudi Arabia recklessly bombed Sana’a airport, to prevent an Iranian plane with a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis subsequently began attacking Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure, and launched a ground offensive against the Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. The Houthi attacks pose the biggest security challenge to Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince and the main architect of the war on Yemen, in decades. Massive Saudi air strikes have neither defeated the Houthis nor restored the kingdom’s deterrence. With its wealth, natural resources, infrastructure and tenuous palace politics, the kingdom remains exposed to Houthi missile and drone attacks, with few good options for a way out. India must prepare a contingency plan for worst-case scenarios. Its immediate priority should be to evacuate stranded Indian pilgrims. It should also articulate a stronger position for stability and work with Arab countries and Tehran to push for a diplomatic settlement to the Iran crisis . For peace to prevail in the Persian Gulf, the guns directed at Iran must first fall silent.

articles.title: Falling short: on Marco Rubio’s second visit to India
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Marco Rubio’s second visit to India this year yielded little in terms of results

The United States Secretary of State’s three-day visit to India , his second in five months, came at a significant time in U.S. politics. Marco Rubio’s Mumbai trip this week was just ahead of the U.S. midterm elections , which would mark the midpoint of President Donald Trump’s second term in office — a point at which the incumbent normally begins to focus on legacy, and possible contenders for the next Presidential election (Mr. Rubio is expected to be one), and start to look for possible partners and friendships around the world. In addition, his visit also raised hopes in New Delhi of a reset in bilateral ties, battered by two years of uncertainty over the Trump administration’s actions. This would include positive moves towards concluding the Bilateral Trade Agreement , reassuring India about U.S. sanctions on the import of Russian oil, preparations for upcoming Trump meets with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Manila (ASEAN) and Miami (G-20) summits, discussing plans for the Quad Summit (on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit) that India has been trying to host, and setting a date for Mr. Trump’s India visit. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar’s invitation also offered Mr. Rubio an opportunity to meet their UAE counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, to discuss the Gulf situation and to restore energy security and connectivity. And finally, Mr. Rubio’s visit to the Jamnagar Reliance refinery, led to speculation of some major deals on energy, possibly offering more discounts as he pitched for India to buy more American and U.S.-licensed Venezuelan oil.

Given all the high expectations, the visit was bound to come up short. The optics of his visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar, but not New Delhi, which was announced by the U.S. Ambassador to India , gave the Opposition fodder to question the real purpose of the visit. Despite Mr. Rubio’s two visits to India and more than six by Mr. Jaishankar to the U.S. since Mr. Trump took office, relations remain on edge, with issues on trade, tariffs, H-1B restrictions and anti-immigrant measures unaddressed. Also, the U.S.’s narrative on Operation Sindoor (2025), growing ties with Pakistan, and the Trump administration’s rhetoric on India’s economy, diaspora and Russian oil trade have added to India’s unhappiness. The two sides did not announce any agreements and Mr. Jaishankar and Mr. Rubio did not hold a joint press address. However, as they did at the U.S. Independence Day’s 250th anniversary celebrations in Delhi in May, they attended the “Freedom 250” event in Mumbai. Mr. Rubio acknowledged that while no two countries would agree on all issues, he said the U.S.-India alignment on core issues of national interest was “extraordinary” . From this point on, Mr. Rubio must walk that talk, with a view to ensuring that India-U.S. ties are able to move on from the difficulties of the last few years.

Mr. Rubio acknowledged that while no two countries would agree on all issues, he said the U.S.-India alignment on core issues of national interest was “extraordinary” . articles.title: Canary in the coal mine: On the performance of India’s core industrial sectors
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Core sector data indicate impending growth slowdowns

The latest data on the performance of the core industrial sectors show the economy may be facing an industrial uptick, but questions about its sustainability remain. Growth in the Index of Core Industries rose to a series-high of 7.9% in September 2026, the second consecutive month of accelerated performance. Any such improvement is to be celebrated, but a deeper look at what is driving it is also warranted. The coal sector saw growth suddenly shoot up to 10.7% in September. The unexpected and unusual nature of this rapid acceleration can be borne out by the fact that the sector contracted by 1.1% over the longer April-September 2026 period. The growth in coal in September was likely a temporary blip aided by a statistical low base and, more importantly, pressure from power plant operators over rapidly depleting coal stocks amid the heat wave. The electricity sector grew 11.4% in September, capping off a half-year dominated by double-digit growth. This surge in electricity-related demand for coal will likely wane, especially since the El Niño factor that drove the heat wave will also result in a milder winter. The other sector that results in high coal usage, the steel sector, did accelerate in September, but not by enough to sustain the coal sector’s September output. The uptick in steel did, however, result in a return to double-digit growth for the iron ore sector, which should bode well for the mining component of the larger Index of Industrial Production.

The performance of the crude oil, natural gas, and refinery products sectors also highlights the fiscal problems India faces. At a time when the crude oil and natural gas sectors have both contracted continuously since 2024, refinery output rose to 10.3% in September. This means that the refineries were increasingly processing expensive imported oil. India’s oil imports in September were up 7% by volume but jumped 47% in terms of value due to the high price of oil. This is set to worsen. The attacks on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure have already pushed global oil prices above $112 a barrel, almost a six-month high. The reprieve from the U.S. on potential tariffs linked to imports of Russian oil provide India a reliable source, but the days of discounts are long gone. It is the time of premium pricing, and each barrel imported is eating into India’s foreign exchange reserves, which are also being used to defend the rupee. Cement and steel are the only sustainably growing core sectors, and those too are based on government infrastructure spending. At a time when industrial output is only temporarily propped up, the government’s fiscal space is fast shrinking.

articles.title: Tunnelling through: On China’s export control list, tunnel-boring machines
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Domestic manufacturing and foreign partnerships must go hand-in-hand

The Chinese Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs decision to place tunnel-boring machines (TBMs) on an export control list reveals a blind spot in India’s supply chain diversification. The curbs include TBMs, walking excavators, and high-altitude wet shotcrete machines. From November 18, if a shipment is intended for countries or regions deemed sensitive due to ongoing disputes with China, exporters will need an export licence from commerce authorities. For other countries/regions, exporters will need to be registered, obtain an export certificate, and submit end-use declarations stating that the equipment will not be re-routed to sensitive locations. While China has cornered around 70% of the global TBM market, prominent manufacturers in the West also maintain substantial component supply chains in the country to cut manufacturing overhead. Further, TBMs are complex to build as they have to be configured to geological characteristics at the project site and perform numerous tasks. Where a suitable TBM exists, it can be used for civilian or military purposes. India has struggled with TBM-related hold-ups with China for at least two years now, including for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project. Germany’s Herrenknecht AG set up an assembling and refurbishing facility in Chennai in 2007-08. TBM production economics differ significantly from conventional construction equipment as new plants need a minimum number of orders and must be able to access the industrial capability required to design, manufacture and repair specialised components.

However, even though India is one of the world’s largest TBM importers, expecting every sophisticated machine to be produced domestically will send public infrastructure costs soaring. Even now, depending on China’s decision on the TBMs set for India, India may have to redirect its procurement to facilities based directly in Germany or Japan, say, and absorb the higher capital cost. The BEML experience shows that manufacturing partnerships can fail without secure licensing arrangements and access to sustained demand. India should pursue domestic manufacturing alongside international partnerships, e.g., making equipment in the country under agreement with established foreign firms, and develop shared industrial capabilities rather than singular ‘national champions’, as TBM manufacturers and their suppliers can benefit from access to common testing and precision manufacturing infrastructure. Overall, Beijing is systematically identifying sectors where it commands a significant global capacity and establishing export controls to counter western technological restrictions, such as on advanced semiconductors, so any critical infrastructure sector relying on Chinese supply lines will face a compounding geopolitical risk.

articles.title: Ethanol tender sparks feedstock concerns as rice gains ground over maize
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: The competing concerns highlight the challenge facing the ethanol procurement framework: balancing the availability and cost of different feedstocks.

The Oil Marketing Companies’ (OMCs) latest ethanol procurement tender for Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2026–27 has triggered concerns among grain-based ethanol producers and sections of the sugar industry over feedstock pricing, allocation priorities and the potential implications for the sector.

The tender sets procurement prices at ₹60.32 a litre for surplus foodgrains (SFG), with a stated cap of 108 crore litres for the first three quarters; ₹64 a litre for damaged foodgrains (DFG); and ₹66 a litre for maize, plus an additional ₹2.79 a litre. While ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses has been excluded, C-heavy molasses-based ethanol remains eligible for procurement.

The Grain Ethanol Manufacturers Association (GEMA) has argued that the tender places a disproportionate burden on rice-based feedstocks, particularly SFG and DFG, while potentially weakening maize’s role as an industrial feedstock.
The pricing differential has also created uncertainty over how procurement demand will be distributed among the different feedstock categories.

articles.title: Data suggests broad-based increase in food prices: RBI Bulletin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: Inflation in rural areas was found to be higher than in urban areas; headline CPI inflation edged up over the months and showed signs of greater generalisation across commodities

High-frequency data collected by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for October (till 19th), suggest a broad-based increase in food prices, said RBI officials in the October edition of RBI Bulletin, which was released on Friday (October 23, 2026).

“Among cereals, rice and wheat prices continued to increase. Prices of major pulses also went up sequentially. Edible oil prices also recorded a slow and broad-based increase, led by mustard and palm oil,” they wrote in the ‘State of the Economy’ article.
Among vegetables, while potato prices declined and the pace of onion price increases dropped, tomato prices picked up, they added.

Surprisingly, inflation in rural areas has been getting higher than that in urban areas. Inflation stood at 4.9% and 6.1%, respectively, in urban and rural areas in September. In August, urban and rural inflation stood at 4.3% and 5.2% respectively, the officials stated.
ALSO WATCH The battle against inflation is entering a tougher phase: What it means for you

The majority of States/UTs recorded inflation in the range of 4-6% in September. Inflation ranged from 2.9% to 6.9% across states/UTs. States like Telangana, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry recorded inflation in excess of 6% across both rural and urban areas, they pointed out.

Stating that WPI inflation recorded its first double-digit rate in the new series (Base 2022-23) at 11.4% in September 2026, rising from 9.9% in August, reflecting a broad-based increase in prices, they said industrial and farm input costs remained elevated.
Inflation in the Output Producer Price Index surged to 11.4% in September 2026 from 9.8% in August, led by manufacturing products, and mining & quarrying, they said.
As per the article headline, CPI inflation edged up over the months and showed signs of greater generalisation across commodities, calling for a commensurate change in the monetary policy stance.
“The external headwinds are also being dealt with a slew of regulatory measures by the Reserve Bank to curb speculative activity in foreign exchange market,” they stated.

“Strong inflows under FCNR(B) swap window augmented reserves. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) and remittance flows strengthened in August. With strong exports growth, the trade deficit narrowed in September,” they added.

The headline Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation rose to a 23-month high of 5.5% (YoY) in September from 4.8% in August, driven by a broad-based increase in food, fuel and core (CPI excluding food and fuel) components.

articles.title: Minister Vanni Arasu inspects rain affected areas in Kallakurichi
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Minister for Social Justice Vanni Arasu inspected rain-affected areas in Kallakurichi district and directed officials to strengthen precautionary measures.

Accompanied by Collector J.E. Padmaja, the Minister visited Porasakurichi and Virugavur villages in Thiyagadurgam block. He said the district administration had taken precautionary measures for the Northeast monsoon.

He instructed officials to identify vulnerable areas, monitor preparedness and respond immediately to rain-related problems. They were also asked to compile details of local volunteers and coordinate with them during emergencies.

The Minister also directed Health department personnel to monitor all areas to prevent outbreaks of infectious diseases. Officials were told to ensure chlorinated drinking water, uninterrupted electricity supply and prompt delivery of essential services. Calls received at the district control room should be attended to immediately and referred to the departments concerned for action, he said.

articles.title: State government relaxes norms for height restriction on non-high rise buildings
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The State government has amended the Tamil Nadu Combined Development and Building Rules, 2019, relaxing height restriction on non-high rise buildings from 18.3 metres to 19.5 metres
The State government has amended the Tamil Nadu Combined Development and Building Rules, 2019, relaxing the height restriction on non-high rise buildings from 18.3 metres to 19.5 metres.
Previously, any building exceeding 18.3 metres in height was categorised as a high rise building requiring stringent norms for construction, when compared with non-high rise buildings.

Owing to the restrictions in height of 18.3 metres for non high rise buildings, many builders have been facing issues in receiving completion certificates of homes in the non-high rise category. Owing to the new amendment, homes will get better ventilation and aesthetics, with improved height of ceiling.

According to the amendment, sites abutting and gaining access from roads of width 12 metres and above shall be deemed to have been zoned for commercial use zone for Chennai Metropolitan Area and sites abutting and gaining access from roads of width 9 metres and above shall be deemed to have been zoned as commercial use zone for the rest of Tamil Nadu.
The minimum road width for buildings including conference halls, exclusive multi storeyed parking lots and air conditioned cinema theatre with single screen is 12 metres.

The minimum road width for exhibition halls, community halls, kalyana mandapams in municipal corporations and municipalities will be 15 metre while the road width will be 12 metres in Town panchayats and village panchayats.
The minimum road width for star hotels and multiplexes or malls will be 18 metres.

The qualifying road width shall be available continuously for a length of 100 metres from any one side of the site or combined on both sides and shall be calculated excluding the plot frontage of the site. There shall be a road intersection within the said 100-metre stretch; where there is no such intersection within the said 100-metre stretch, the qualifying road width shall be available continuously for a minimum length of 3,250 metres in areas falling within the Chennai Metropolitan Area and the municipal corporations and for a minimum length of 100 metres in all other areas. The prescribed road stretch abutting the site may be straight or curved, zigzag, or a combination of the above.
The amendments have also changed the rules pertaining to swimming pools.

articles.title: A.P., Odisha on alert as cyclone ‘Arnab’ nears land | LIVE
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: IMD issues red alerts for seven of the 28 districts in Andhra Pradesh for October 27

The Odisha government announced the closure of all educational institutions in six southern districts and started moving people from vulnerable areas to safety as severe cyclonic storm Arnab headed towards making landfall on October 28.

In its latest bulletin, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said the cyclone was very likely to continue to move west-northwestwards and intensify further into a very severe cyclonic storm over the same region during the next 12 hours.

“It is very likely to cross Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam as a very severe cyclonic storm with the maximum sustained wind speed of 115-125 kmph gusting up to 140 kmph by the forenoon of October 28.”
Severe cyclone Arnab nears Andhra coast, prompting red alerts for seven districts amid heavy rainfall, high winds, and disaster preparedness in AP.

The eastern coastal states of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh closed schools, prohibited sea fishing and kept rescue teams on standby, stepping up precautionary measures ahead of Cyclone Arnab’s expected landfall on Wednesday to ensure “zero loss of life and minimal damage to infrastructure”.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD), in its Monday morning bulletin, said a deep depression over east-central and southeast Bay of Bengal has moved westward and has intensified into cyclonic storm ‘Arnab’.

The Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority has issued toll-free helpline numbers for emergency assistance. People can contact the State Emergency Operations Centre (SEOC) at 112, 1070 or 1800 425 0101 for help.

The India Meteorological Department has forecast isolated extremely heavy rainfall over Coastal Andhra Pradesh and Yanam on October 27–28, Odisha on October 28, Chhattisgarh on October 28–29, and east Uttar Pradesh on October 29.

Cyclone ‘Arnab’, over the central Bay of Bengal, has moved at 13 kmph over the past six hours and is expected to intensify into a severe cyclone shortly. It is currently centred 540 km from Visakhapatnam, 620 km from Kakinada, 720 km from Machilipatnam and 790 km from Bapatla.

Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority said the cyclone has moved at a speed of 13 km per hour over the past 6 hours. Currently, it is centered 580 km from Visakhapatnam, 660 km from Kakinada, 760 km from Machilipatnam, and 830 km from Bapatla. ​ ​
In the last 24 hours ending 6 a.m. on Monday (October 26, 2026), Rameswaram, Pamban, Thangachimadam and R.S. Mangalam in Ramanathapuram district recorded over 100 mm rainfall.
Normal life was hit badly as overnight rains lashed many parts of the district.

articles.title: Tiger Shroff firing case: Custody of four accused extended till Oct 28; 11th accused remanded till Oct 31
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Mumbai Crime Branch seeks to trace weapon supply, Signal communications and local support network; defence questions need for further custody

A Mumbai court on Monday (October 26, 2026) extended the police custody of four accused in the firing case involving Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff’s car by two days, till October 28. The Mumbai Crime Branch had sought an extension till October 31 to investigate alleged local support, recover communication data and collect voice samples. Meanwhile, the ninth and tenth accused were also remanded in police custody till October 28, taking the total number of arrests in the case to 11.

The four accused, arrested on October 23, were produced before the court on Monday (October 26, 2026) after their earlier police custody ended. Investigators sought further custody to establish how the accused allegedly coordinated through the encrypted messaging application Signal, trace the source of firearms and ammunition, and identify those who may have assisted them in Mumbai.

Advocates Omkar Inamdar and Ajinkya Mirgal, appearing for the accused, opposed the extension, arguing that investigators had already been granted sufficient time to interrogate their clients and recover evidence.

The defence submitted that mobile phones, SIM cards, bank details and debit cards had already been recovered. Mr. Inamdar said the accused had undergone interrogation during their three-day transit remand and subsequent police custody, questioning the need for further detention.

The lawyers also disputed the relevance of photographs and personal conversations recovered from the phones, maintaining that the images were selfies with friends and that the conversations did not appear connected to the alleged offence.

According to the defence, investigators reiterated their earlier grounds concerning communications allegedly exchanged through Signal. Police also sought voice samples from all four accused, which the lawyers argued could be collected during judicial custody with the court’s permission.

The defence further questioned the need for additional custody to identify the accused’s alleged local support network, arguing that investigators who had travelled across States to make arrests should have been able to establish whether they received assistance in Mumbai.

The lawyers also challenged the prosecution’s allegation that the accused intended to bring a weapon into Mumbai and subsequently take it back. They pointed to the recovery of a firearm from Surat, Gujarat, arguing that questions concerning its connection to the alleged offence could be examined during trial.
The court, however, granted two additional days of police custody.
Meanwhile, advocate Ajinkya Mirgal said the ninth and tenth accused arrested in the case had been produced before a court and remanded in police custody till October 28.
According to Mirgal, investigators are questioning them about the source of the weapons, alleged logistical assistance, the wider conspiracy behind the firing and possible gang connections.

In a separate development, 22-year-old Pranjal Thakran, a resident of Kharkhoda in Haryana’s Sonipat district, was arrested in Indore on Saturday (October 24, 2026), in a joint operation by the Mumbai Crime Branch and Indore Crime Branch.

articles.title: A final surge: On Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s triumph in Brazil
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Lula is the resistance to U.S. imperial ambitions in South America

At one point, it seemed almost impossible for Brazil’s 80-year-old President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to turn the tide after finishing second to Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of elections on October 4. In Brazil’s history, no candidate who has finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidential run-off. Most of the candidates who dropped out after the first round were from the right. Flávio’s Liberal Party cemented its position in both houses of Congress, while right-wing candidates won several provincial elections. But Lula, a former trade unionist and organiser, who lost a finger in an accident as a teenager, was not ready to give up. Lula and his Workers’ Party identified campaign weaknesses, shifted their attention to economic issues, promised growth and welfare, and persuaded more voters to turn out for Sunday’s run-off. Lula won 51.7% of the vote against Flávio’s 48.2%, a greater lead than his victory against Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio’s father, four years ago. Over the weeks, Lula turned the right-wing’s gains in the first round against it, highlighting the threats that a Bolsonaro victory could pose to democracy and civil rights. Flávio’s campaign pledge to free his father — he is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn Lula’s 2022 victory, and impeach Supreme Court judges — only heightened the concerns of voters outside the right wing, who rallied behind a familiar face.

Lula unleashed a social media campaign to mobilise younger voters. A WhatsApp channel called ‘Lula’s Army’ with 11 million followers spread his message of continuity. He also announced plans to expand a cash payout scheme for the poor, a new debt relief package and entrepreneur-friendly measures. In the northeast, the Workers’ Party’s stronghold, he gained nearly three million votes and made considerable gains in the working-class neighbourhoods of big cities, including São Paulo. A relatively stable economic record, marked by growth and falling unemployment over the past three and a half years, also lent credibility to Lula’s appeal. His victory bucks the recent trend in South America, where Washington-aligned right-wing and conservative forces have gained ground. While Lula offers predictable stability and social and economic inclusiveness, he could also be, as the President of South America’s largest economy, a voice of resistance to Donald Trump’s imperial ambitions. At the same time, Lula will have to work with a right-wing-controlled Congress to advance his agenda. He should seek to build legislative consensus while focusing on addressing the economic challenges of Brazil, which remains one of the most unequal major world economies.

articles.title: Dubious retreat: On the National Medical Commission and its MSMER
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The National Medical Commission must not be seen as lax on regulation

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has denotified and withdrawn its 2023 Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations (MSMER ), diminishing the framework of penalties vis-à-vis educational standards and infrastructure at medical colleges. The move is noteworthy as the MSMER provided for fines of up to ₹5 lakh on faculty members and administrators for submitting false information. Fortunately, the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) retains the power to fine errant institutions up to ₹1 crore under the 2023 Establishment of Medical Institutions, Assessment and Rating Regulations . MSMER was lauded for its intention to crack down on the deep-seated corruption and malpractice in medical colleges, particularly over ‘ghost faculty’ and ‘ghost patients’. The NMC’s justification is that MSMER also introduced a parallel mechanism allowing undergraduate and postgraduate boards to evaluate institutions, stepping on the MARB’s toes. However, why the NMC scrapped MSMER wholesale is unclear. The 2023 Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations remain in force and include a provision to fine individual faculty members at postgraduate medical colleges. Non-compliance among medical colleges is not uncommon and seldom nipped in the bud, even as the number of medical seats swells while the transparency of the medical education system has not improved.

Notwithstanding the provision to fine individuals at postgraduate centres, the MARB and the NMC can only penalise institutions, which is harder and risks creating a perverse incentive to accommodate rather than punish, and could mitigate the fear that keeps administrators honest. MSMER also specified timelines to appeal penalties. Although the MARB regulations retain the appeal processes, their 15-day deadline could conflict with the 60-day period under the NMC Act, potentially creating legal disputes that delay penal action. There is also a telling incident. As part of a proceeding under the RTI Act, the Central Information Commission revealed last year that the NMC had stated in 2024 that MARB had neither formally assessed nor rated medical colleges and that its standard forms need not be made public. In a revised reply in October 2025, it said the responding NMC officer’s records did not include any of the corresponding reports. However, the 2023 MARB regulations require the Board to publish its latest annual assessment results. If the NMC withdrew MSMER because the powers thereunder also exist elsewhere, the public deserves to know whether the powers are also being exercised and whether the outcomes are as publicly accessible as intended. Unless the NMC has satisfactory answers for all these lacunae, the withdrawal will appear less like simplification and more like regulatory relaxation.

As part of a proceeding under the RTI Act, the Central Information Commission revealed last year that the NMC had stated in 2024 that MARB had neither formally assessed nor rated medical colleges and that its standard forms need not be made public. In a revised reply in October 2025, it said the responding NMC officer’s records did not include any of the corresponding reports. However, the 2023 MARB regulations require the Board to publish its latest annual assessment results. If the NMC withdrew MSMER because the powers thereunder also exist elsewhere, the public deserves to know whether the powers are also being exercised and whether the outcomes are as publicly accessible as intended. Unless the NMC has satisfactory answers for all these lacunae, the withdrawal will appear less like simplification and more like regulatory relaxation.

articles.title: Media association challenges privacy law in Supreme Court
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: A three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant is scheduled to hear a batch of petitions filed by activists on October 27

The Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), which has members drawn from across the media spectrum, including those owned by the Ambani and Adani Groups, have challenged the Union government’s privacy law as a violation of journalistic freedom.
A three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant is scheduled to hear a batch of petitions filed by activists on October 27.

The petition filed by the DNPA, which is also listed before the Bench, challenged specific provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025.
The DNPA said the law was completely in contravention with the law laid down by the Supreme Court in its privacy judgment, which held the right inviolable and fundamental to human dignity and life.
“They impermissibly restrict the fundamental right to information and freedom of speech and expression,” the petition said.

The law fails “to provide any exemption in favour of journalistic activity as a distinct class of processing, entitled to constitutional protection under Article 14 and 19(l)(a) of the Constitution of India and threatens the full spectrum of Journalistic activity carried out by journalists, ground reporters, citizens, whistleblowers, RTI activists, and other stakeholders, and strikes at the core of our democratic framework and runs contrary to the basic tenets of the Constitution of India,” the petition said.
It said publishers, editors, reporters and correspondents were, as a consequence of the law, brought within a regime of notice and prior consent, compelled erasure, and verifiable consent.

Section 36 of the DPDP Act, read with Rule 23 and the Seventh Schedule of the DPDP Rules, vested the Central government with an unbridled and standardless authority to requisition any information from any data fiduciary or intermediary, unaccompanied by judicial oversight, any requirement of necessity or proportionality, or notice to the affected data principal.
“Such a power is capable of being turned to the identification and targeting of journalistic sources and is thus constitutionally infirm,” the petition said.
Section 44 (3) of the DPDP Act, by amending Section 8 (1 )(j) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, has placed every category of “personal information” beyond the reach of disclosure.
Further, by amending the Right to Information Act 2005, the DPDP Act has created an absolute bar on the seeking of information relating to public offices.

articles.title: SHRC calls for checks on private clinics after boy’s death following tonsil surgery in Kannur
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Commission issued the directive to the Additional Chief Secretary, Health department, asking the authorities to verify the qualifications and registration of doctors and other staff working at such clinics.

The Kerala State Human Rights Commission (SHRC) has directed the Health department to ensure that private clinical establishments comply with prescribed standards and to take legal action against those violating the rules. The directive follows the death of a 17-year-old boy after tonsil surgery at a clinic in Kannur in July 2024.

The Commission issued the directive to the Additional Chief Secretary, Health department, asking the authorities to verify the qualifications and registration of doctors and other staff working at such clinics. It also called for guidelines to ensure the quality of medical services and patient safety, along with an effective monitoring mechanism.

The Commission directed the State Police Chief to order a further investigation into the case registered by the Kannur Town police, under the supervision of a Crime Branch officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police. The investigation should comprehensively examine alleged lapses in treatment, allegations of alterations to medical and nursing records, the qualifications and registration of the doctor who performed the surgery, and the registration status of the clinical establishments concerned, the Commission said.

The order followed a complaint filed by P. Shaji, a native of Kannadiparamba and the boy’s father, over the death of his son. The boy died after undergoing tonsil surgery at a clinic in Kannur on July 17, 2024.

An investigation conducted by the Commission’s inquiry wing, headed by its Inspector General, found that the doctor who operated on the boy did not have the legal authorisation to practise in Keralam. The inquiry report also found that neither the clinic where the surgery was performed nor the clinic to which the boy was subsequently admitted had obtained registration as required under the rules.

The Commission noted discrepancies between the reports of inquiries conducted into the incident under the leadership of the district medical officer. It also observed in its order that there had been culpable negligence in the boy’s death.

articles.title: Two Vande Bharat trains partially cancelled for signal work at Kalamassery station on Oct. 27
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Two Vande Bharat services to be partially cancelled, while the Mangala Lakshadweep Superfast Express will be delayed by 90 minutes
The following train services will be regulated on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) due to major signal infrastructure improvement work at Kalamassery railway station.

The following train services will be partially cancelled— Train No. 26651, KSR Bengaluru-Ernakulam Junction Vande Bharat Express, leaving KSR Bengaluru on October 27, will be short-terminated at Thrissur. The service between Thrissur and Ernakulam Junction will remain cancelled.

Train No. 26652, Ernakulam Junction-KSR Bengaluru Vande Bharat Express, scheduled to leave Ernakulam Junction on the same day, will commence its journey from Thrissur as per the regular schedule. The service between Ernakulam Junction and Thrissur will remain cancelled.

Train No. 12617, Ernakulam Junction-Hazrat Nizamuddin Mangala Lakshadweep Superfast Express, scheduled to leave Ernakulam Junction at 1.25 p.m., will be rescheduled to depart at 2.55 p.m., a delay of one hour and 30 minutes.

articles.title: BJP holds nationwide protests against Congress president’s 'derogatory' remarks on PM Modi’s late father
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: BJP leaders and workers protested near Sena Bhawan Circle and on Rajaji Marg, close to Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge’s residence, in Delhi

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Monday (October 26, 2026) staged nationwide protests against what it described as “derogatory” remarks made by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge regarding Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s late father.

BJP workers held demonstrations in Delhi, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Karnataka, West Bengal, Telangana, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Kerala, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Rajasthan, and Chhattisgarh, demanding a public apology from the Congress leadership.

In Delhi, BJP leaders and workers protested near Sena Bhawan Circle and on Rajaji Marg, close to Mr. Kharge’s residence. State BJP president and Union Minister of State Harsh Malhotra, along with other party leaders, participated in the protest. In Bihar’s Patna, party workers took out a “Jan Akrosh March” under the leadership of State BJP chief Sanjay Saraogi.

In Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh Deputy Chief Minister Brajesh Pathak demanded an apology from the Congress leadership over the remarks. In Jammu & Kashmir, workers of the Bharatiya Janata Yuva Morcha also expressed their outrage, while a “dharna” was held at Freedom Park in Bengaluru. In Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, a demonstration was organised under the leadership of State BJP president Rajeev Chandrasekhar.
Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami and Union Minister of State Arjun Ram Meghwal also voiced their objections.

articles.title: A ready solution to tackle anaemia
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Double fortified salt offers a scalable solution to one of India’s most pressing public health challenges

Despite significant economic progress and sustained public health efforts, anaemia — driven significantly by iron deficiency — continues to be one of India’s most pressing public health challenges. Affecting over half of Indian women and almost three-fourths of children, anaemia contributes to maternal mortality, an intergenerational cycle of malnutrition, impaired cognitive development, reduced productivity and substantial economic losses. The Government of India’s 7X7X7 Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy, which was launched recently, rightly recognises the multifactorial nature of anaemia through a comprehensive approach spanning prevention, screening, treatment, dietary diversification and behaviour change. Yet, one proven preventive intervention remains significantly underutilised.

That intervention is Double Fortified Salt (DFS) — salt fortified with both iodine and iron. Salt offers an unparalleled opportunity to address iron deficiency. Consumed daily by virtually every household across India, in predictable quantities regardless of income or geography, it is uniquely suited to deliver a preventive nutrition intervention at population scale. DFS also addresses one of the fundamental challenges of anaemia control — sustained compliance.

Delivering iron through an everyday food complements interventions such as iron supplementation and dietary diversification, whose effectiveness depends on regular adherence. India already has one of the world’s most successful public health platforms in Universal Salt Iodisation, with around 95% of households consuming iodised salt. Building on this existing infrastructure, DFS is already distributed to an estimated 76 million people across four States through government safety-net programmes. Global and Indian evidence strongly support DFS. A global review has shown that DFS can reduce anaemia by up to 21%. Randomised controlled trials in Bengaluru, Darjeeling, and Punjab, along with large-scale implementation in Uttar Pradesh, have shown improvements in iron status and confirmed that, when manufactured to validated specifications, DFS is acceptable to consumers, reduces iron deficiency, and is highly cost-effective. A DFS standard has been issued by the Government of India’s Food Safety and Standards Authority (FSSAI), and the Government of India actually mandates DFS’ inclusion in the national school feeding programme (PM POSHAN and the national early childhood development programme- Integrated Child Development Scheme, or ICDS).

At an estimated cost of ₹14-₹20 per person annually, DFS represents one of the most affordable population-level nutrition interventions available, with a benefit-cost ratio of 4.2:1 for national DFS introduction, primarily driven by improved health outcomes and subsequent increases in labour productivity. India also possesses the manufacturing capacity to produce high-quality DFS at scale. Established fortification technologies, centralised salt production and existing laboratory infrastructure make quality assurance and regulatory monitoring simpler than for many other fortified foods.

What has limited DFS from wider adoption? The barriers are now primarily institutional rather than technical. The next imperative is to accelerate its nationwide adoption and ensure last-mile access, particularly the Public Distribution System apart from social safety-net programmes, across all States through a central flagship scheme. Although DFS is recommended under PM POSHAN and ICDS, its integration into the largest safety net programme i.e., the Public Distribution System (PDS) — which reaches around 800 million beneficiaries — remains uneven because implementation depends largely on State governments. Greater policy commitment, dedicated financing, stronger quality assurance, wider commercial availability and consumer awareness are now needed to accelerate nationwide scale-up. These are implementation challenges — not technological ones — and are well within India’s capacity to address.

Like all public health nutrition interventions, DFS should be implemented within a robust regulatory framework. It should complement existing strategies under Anaemia Mukt Bharat, align with India’s sodium reduction goals, and continue to be accompanied by screening for haemoglobinopathies such as thalassaemia and sickle cell disease. These safeguards are well recognised through experience of rice fortification programme and can be readily integrated into implementation and monitoring systems.
The launch of the revised AMB strategy provides renewed momentum to strengthen the preventive pillar of India’s anaemia response and advance the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.

India has already shown the world how science, policy, public systems, and public awareness can transform nutrition through Universal Salt Iodisation. By scaling DFS nationally, India can not only accelerate progress towards Anaemia Mukt Bharat but also contribute to global efforts to reduce iron deficiency by demonstrating an affordable, scalable model for other low- and middle-income countries.

Marthi Venkatesh Mannar is former Senior Advisor, Tata Trusts; K.J. Alphons is a former Union Minister for State, Government of India; Jaykumar Menon is Co-Founder and Chair, Open Source Pharma Foundation; Dr. Rajiv Tandon is Executive Director, The Health Continuum, Adjunct Professor of Public Health Practice at the Public Health Foundation of India, Indian Institutes of Public Health, and Ruchika Arora is Technical Specialist, The Health Continuum and former national consultant for child health and Nutrition, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

articles.title: CEC can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge, ECI tells top court
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: A common affidavit filed for the EC, CEC Kumar and Election Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi say that any attempt to restrain the CEC’s functioning is contrary to the 2023 Act; asserts that Form 6 was not amended; West Bengal CEO’s officers filed appeals against inclusions

The Election Commission of India, Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the two Election Commissioners have filed a joint affidavit highlighting that any attempt to restrain the functioning of the CEC will be contrary to law.

The nearly 250-page document filed in the top court late on Monday (October 26, 2026) said a CEC cannot be removed from office except in the manner and the grounds identical to ousting a Supreme Court judge.

The affidavit said a media report on the inner frictions and alleged unilateral or authoritarian functioning of the CEC was hardly evidence in court. Petitions basing itself on media reports should not be even maintainable in court.

Petitioners who have challenged the functioning of the CEC include the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and other INDIA bloc leaders. Other petitioners include Rakesh Kumar Singh and advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi.

The affidavit, which shows the CEC to be on the same page as both Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, said the Commission had “neither released nor authorised the release of any internal note or file to any news agency”.

They submitted that the multi-member Commission, in case of any “difference of opinion” would follow the rule of majority to arrive at decisions in accordance with Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
The affidavit indicated that there was no room for unilateral decision making in the ECI. Decisions were vetted at various levels.

“Decisions are first sent to one Election Commissioner and then to the other Election Commissioner and then finally to the CEC. Such approved decisions of the EC are duly noted in the files concerned of the EC and bear the signature of the Election Commissioners and the CEC. Thereafter, the decision is notified and implemented by the EC Secretariat,” the affidavit said.

However, the ECI concedes in the affidavit at one point that “in situations involving exigencies and particularly where the immediate issuance of appropriate orders is necessary, when it is not feasible for the CEC or any of the Election Commissioners to be available in person”, an approval of the members of the ECI is obtained through “electronic means” and recorded later in the official file.

“Important functions” were “directly under the Commission as a whole”. “Decisions taken in meetings of the EC or are noted in files bear the signatures of the Election Commissioners and the CEC,” the affidavit said.
An office order was issued on July 28, 2026 by an IAS officer of the rank of additional secretary who had been posted on deputation to the ECI pertaining to internal work allocation.

The affidavit, however, indirectly confirmed that Mr. Sandhu and Mr. Joshi had written to the Cabinet Secretary about the conduct of Senior Deputy Election Commissioner Maneesh Garg, following a controversial July 28 order affecting levels of IT oversight over electoral rolls. The order was passed without the knowledge or consensus of the two Election Commissioners.

A common affidavit filed for the EC, CEC Kumar and Election Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi say that any attempt to restrain the CEC’s functioning is contrary to the 2023 Act; asserts that Form 6 was not amended; West Bengal CEO’s officers filed appeals against inclusions

The Election Commission of India, Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the two Election Commissioners have filed a joint affidavit highlighting that any attempt to restrain the functioning of the CEC will be contrary to law.

The nearly 250-page document filed in the top court late on Monday (October 26, 2026) said a CEC cannot be removed from office except in the manner and the grounds identical to ousting a Supreme Court judge.

The affidavit said a media report on the inner frictions and alleged unilateral or authoritarian functioning of the CEC was hardly evidence in court. Petitions basing itself on media reports should not be even maintainable in court.

Petitioners who have challenged the functioning of the CEC include the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and other INDIA bloc leaders. Other petitioners include Rakesh Kumar Singh and advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi.

The affidavit, which shows the CEC to be on the same page as both Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, said the Commission had “neither released nor authorised the release of any internal note or file to any news agency”.

They submitted that the multi-member Commission, in case of any “difference of opinion” would follow the rule of majority to arrive at decisions in accordance with Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.

The affidavit indicated that there was no room for unilateral decision making in the ECI. Decisions were vetted at various levels.

“Decisions are first sent to one Election Commissioner and then to the other Election Commissioner and then finally to the CEC. Such approved decisions of the EC are duly noted in the files concerned of the EC and bear the signature of the Election Commissioners and the CEC. Thereafter, the decision is notified and implemented by the EC Secretariat,” the affidavit said.

However, the ECI concedes in the affidavit at one point that “in situations involving exigencies and particularly where the immediate issuance of appropriate orders is necessary, when it is not feasible for the CEC or any of the Election Commissioners to be available in person”, an approval of the members of the ECI is obtained through “electronic means” and recorded later in the official file.

“Important functions” were “directly under the Commission as a whole”. “Decisions taken in meetings of the EC or are noted in files bear the signatures of the Election Commissioners and the CEC,” the affidavit said.

An office order was issued on July 28, 2026 by an IAS officer of the rank of additional secretary who had been posted on deputation to the ECI pertaining to internal work allocation.

The affidavit, however, indirectly confirmed that Mr. Sandhu and Mr. Joshi had written to the Cabinet Secretary about the conduct of Senior Deputy Election Commissioner Maneesh Garg, following a controversial July 28 order affecting levels of IT oversight over electoral rolls. The order was passed without the knowledge or consensus of the two Election Commissioners.

articles.title: Arnab becomes ‘very severe cyclonic storm’, light showers begin in north Andhra
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The system may continue to move west-northwestwards till October 27 evening, and thereafter the system may cross the coast, close to Yanam, by October 28, 2026 forenoon.

Srikakulam district has received widespread rain overnight, as the Severe Cyclonic Storm (SCS) ‘Arnab’ strengthened into a Very Severe Cyclonic Storm (VSCS) at around 11.30 p.m. on Monday (October 26, 2026).

According to latest information from the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Amaravati, the system lay centred at 2.30 a.m. over Westcentral Bay of Bengal, at around 300 km southeast of Vishakhapatnam, 360 km east-southeast of Kakinada, 380 km south of Gopalpur of Odisha, 460 km east of Machilipatnam, 530 km east of Bapatla and 920 km west-northwest of Sri Vijaya Puram of the Andaman Islands
The system may continue to move west-northwestwards till October 27 evening, and thereafter the system may cross the coast, close to Yanam, by Wednesday (October 28, 2026) forenoon.

Pointing to the thick cloud formation near the northern part of the State, the weather experts said while the rainfall activity has begun in the north, it will reach the central parts of A.P. by afternoon.

According to information from the Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES), 41 stations in Srikakulam district received light to moderate showers on the intervening night of October 26-27. The highest of 41 mm was recorded in Palasa until 8 a.m.
At 8 a.m., the IMD, Amaravati, has forecast moderate rain, with squally wind speed reaching 50-60 kmph, over Anakapalli, Srikakulam, Visakhapatnam and Vizianagaram districts in the next three hours.

articles.title: JD(U) presses for Anant Singh’s disqualification, Speaker’s office assures ‘quick action’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The NDA Government on Monday also removed Mr. Singh’s wife, former MLA Neelam Devi, from the Government’s 20-point programme committee

Two days after expelling Mokama MLA Anant Singh from the party for “anti-party activities”, Janata Dal (United) State president Umesh Kushwaha on Monday (October 26, 2026) visited the office of the Assembly Speaker to ask about action on the party’s earlier request to rescind his membership from the House. He was assured of “quick action”.

The NDA Government on Monday also removed Mr. Singh’s wife, former MLA Neelam Devi, from the Government’s 20-point programme committee, and later asked her to vacate her official bungalow in Patna by November 25, 2026.

“We had submitted evidence against his (Anant Singh’s) anti-party activities to the Speaker’s office on Sunday, October 25. Today I had come to know the status of action on our request to rescind Mr. Singh’s membership of the House, but since Speaker Prem Kumar was not in the office, the Assembly secretary assured me that quick action will be taken,” Mr. Kushwaha told journalists on the Assembly premises.

He also asserted that “the party runs on discipline, and you all (media persons) know well how he was working and what he was saying for the last few days.” Party sources, though, told The Hindu that the JD(U) had submitted 10 pages of evidence and a video CD to the Speaker, along with the expulsion letter, to prove its point.

On October 24, 2026, the ruling JD(U) had expelled Mr. Singh, the party’s strongman MLA from Mokama, and his wife, Ms. Devi, from the party for six years for their “anti-party activities”, and sought his disqualification from the Assembly.

In the recently concluded State Legislative Council elections for eight seats, Mr. Singh had campaigned hard for Opposition candidate Anuj Kumar Singh in the Patna Graduates’ constituency, instead of the party’s official candidate Neeraj Kumar. The results are scheduled to be announced on October 23.

After his expulsion, Mr. Singh told journalists that “he still honours JD(U) chief Nitish Kumar and will continue to do so, but Mr. Kumar is no longer in command of the party, so the JD(U) is finished now and won’t be able to win even 10 seats in the next Assembly elections”. He added that instead of joining another party, he would launch his “own party”.

On the party’s recommendation, the Government on Monday also removed Ms. Devi from the 20-point programme implementation committee, which had given her the status of a Deputy Minister. The Building Construction Department later served a notice on her, where Mr. Singh too was living, to vacate their official bungalow at 1, Mall Road, Patna, by November 25, 2026.
