articles.title: Madras High Court denies anticipatory bail to Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi in ₹100-crore private schools fraud case
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Justice V. Lakshminarayanan dismisses his advance bail plea in a case being investigated by the Chennai Central Crime Branch police

The Madras High Court on Monday (October 26, 2026) denied anticipatory bail to former School Education Minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi of the DMK in a corruption case after observing that the final destination of over ₹400 crore, allegedly collected towards a ‘party fund’ from over 177 private school managements in the State, could be found out only if he is subjected to custodial interrogation.

Justice V. Lakshminarayanan said he was of the view that grant of advance bail to the former Minister would paralyse the investigation being conducted by the Central Crime Branch for offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

“While protection of individual liberty is a duty of the court, it should be weighed against the society’s need for a corruption-free governmental administration,” he said. Rejecting the petitioner’s argument that all evidence in the case was documentary in nature, and hence, his arrest was not absolutely necessary in such a case, the judge said: “Money trails would still require custodial interrogation in order to establish the intent and identify who had been holding the strings and the final destination of the amount alleged to be involved.”

Further, the judge recorded the submission of State Public Prosecutor R. John Sathyan that the second accused Muthukumar, who was a classmate of the former Minister and also the treasurer of a private schools association through which the ‘party fund’ was collected, was still absconding and his whereabouts could be found out only by interrogating the present petitioner. “The petitioner is a politician, holding a high position. If anticipatory bail is granted before the second accused is apprehended, then it would become a tool for the second accused to avoid the process of the investigation. As the investigation is still at its nascent stage and as new facts are being unearthed, this court is of the view that grant of anticipatory bail would not be fit and proper,” Justice Lakshminarayanan said.

He went on to state that corruption was a grave economic offence. “It not only affects the public exchequer but is also a crime against humanity and directly affects the human rights. In cases such as these, the court has to keep in mind the position that had been occupied by the petitioner and thereby his ability to tamper with the State machineries or influence witnesses.”

He also said courts would generally be slow in granting anticipatory bail in corruption cases, especially when a strong apprehension arose that the petitioner could use the liberty to influence witnesses, hamper investigation, or destroy physical evidence. “In the present case, prima facie, the records reveal that the absconding accused — A2 has been shielded by the petitioner,” he wrote.

The judge said Justices J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan of the Supreme Court had in 2025 held that in corruption cases, anticipatory bail could not be sought as a matter of right, and it could be granted only in cases involving political vendetta, false implications, or manifest frivolity. “None of the exceptions pointed out by Pardiwala J. applies to the facts of the present case,” he concluded.

According to the CCB, the first and second accused were the founder president and treasurer respectively of an unregistered body titled ‘Tamil Nadu Private Schools Association’. They were instrumental in collecting crores of rupees from various private school managements for purposes such as gaining permanent recognition, upgradation , DTCP/CMDA approvals, building related permissions and other government approvals.
Former DMK Minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi arrested in ₹100-crore private schools fraud case
Investigation reveals collection of ‘party fund’ during Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi’s tenure as School Education Minister, CCB tells Madras High Court

The investigating agency claimed the unregistered association was formed in 2024 on the basis of the former Minister’s communication through his personal assistant Valadi Karthick. Mr. Poyyamozhi had participated in the event held for inaugurating the association at Kalaivanar Arangam in Chennai on December 30, 2024. Claiming that it had secured the video footage of the event, the CCB said, the then Minister had “projected” Mr. Arasakumar and Mr. Muthukumar before a large gathering of school correspondents.

Thereafter, all the needs of individual school managements were routed through the first two accused for being placed before the higher government level. So far, “more than 177 victim school managements have come forward and a prima facie amount of ₹17,26,73,650 has been traced. The complete financial trail and ultimate beneficiaries is still under investigation,” the CCB told the court.

articles.title: Virtual autopsy at Kozhikode Medical College Hospital: launch likely to take time
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Forensic Medicine Department has submitted a detailed list of the facilities to be introduced at the hospital, including the staff to be appointed and the equipment to be installed, to the government

The proposed launch of virtual autopsy (virtopsy), an advanced forensic technique, at the Government Medical College Hospital (MCH), Kozhikode, is likely to take some more time as the work in this regard is still in progress.

According to official sources, one of the members from the Department of Forensic Medicine at the hospital recently underwent a month-long training in the subject at the North-Eastern Hill Indira Gandhi Regional Institute of Health and Medical Sciences, Shillong, Meghalaya, which is a pioneer in virtual autopsy in the country.

The department has also submitted a detailed list of the facilities to be introduced at the hospital, including the staff to be appointed and the equipment to be installed, to the government. The sources said that discussions are also ongoing with experts at the All-India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi.

The main objectives of an autopsy are determining the cause and manner of death, establishing identity, and collecting evidence for litigation and investigation. Virtual autopsy reports are almost identical to traditional autopsy reports, the difference is only in the use of advanced imaging instead of invasive dissection. Computed Tomography (CT) and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) technologies are used for this non-invasive procedure, where three-dimensional data of the entire body, or relevant parts, are created to examine the details. However, forensic experts point out that in suspicious or unnatural deaths, a medico-legal autopsy is always mandatory.

According to Health department sources, none of the government hospitals in Keralam follows such a system at present. A.K. Unmesh, Professor, Forensic Medicine, had given a detailed project report (DPR) to the government in December 2025 to set up a virtual autopsy centre at the Government Medical College, Kottayam, where he was working then as the Head of the Department. The DPR had said that setting up such a facility would improve medico-legal services, enhance judicial transparency, reduce the stress of families by offering minimally invasive options, and provide permanent digital evidence for appeals and reviews. The plan was to enhance collaboration between departments such as Radiology and Forensic Medicine, and the judiciary and law enforcement. It was also pointed out that a digital repository of forensic imaging could be created for evidence and academic research. The total projected capital cost was ₹15.5 crore, and the recurring annual cost was estimated to be ₹2.5 crore.
After the United Democratic Front (UDF) came to power in May this year, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan has repeatedly declared that the virtual autopsy system would be first launched in Kozhikode.

articles.title: BPCL shifts crude sourcing towards Middle East as Russian oil loses price edge
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: Russian crude accounted for 37% of their import basket in the second quarter.

Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL) tapped more into Middle Eastern crude as Russian oil lost its price advantage and also due to rising freight costs, with the shift becoming more pronounced in November, Vetsa Ramakrishna Gupta, Director (Finance), told analysts during a post-results call on Monday.

“Our spot crude share remained at around 67% in the second quarter, while Russian grade accounted for approximately 37% of our total crude procurement, both broadly in line with the previous quarter,” Mr. Gupta said, adding that the company increased purchases from the Middle East as supplies from the region improved.

Russia accounted for 37% of BPCL’s crude basket in the September quarter, followed by Saudi Arabia at 19%, Abu Dhabi at 17%, the U.S. at 9% and Oman at 6%. The remaining supplies came from countries contributing 1-4% each.
As of September-end, BPCL held about 22 days of crude inventory, with sourcing requirements tied up through December.
Mr. Gupta said the share of Russian crude in October was expected to remain “more or less the same”, although procurement volumes would be lower for November.

“October, our requirement from Russia slightly came down but in the month of November, the cargoes from Russia significantly reduced due to [reduced] commercial viability [compared to that from Middle East], mainly the increase in the freight,” he said, adding that the company did not receive attractive offers for Russian crude in November.

Russian crude was available at a premium of $12-$13 per barrel over benchmark prices in October. The premium has narrowed to $1-$2 per barrel for December cargoes, Mr. Gupta said, although freight costs remain high.
“Maybe today, Russian cargo is preferable than a Middle Eastern cargo for December month because November [procurement] we have already concluded,” he said.

BPCL also diversified its liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) sourcing during the quarter. Supplies from the Arab Gulf improved, while the US accounted for about 48% of LPG imports in the September quarter.
Softening Saudi Contract Prices (Saudi CP), the benchmark for LPG pricing, helped reduce under-recoveries to an average ₹290 per cylinder in the September quarter from ₹507 in the June quarter.

Under-recoveries are expected to be ₹245 per cylinder in October and are expected to rise to ₹328 in November, Mr. Gupta said. BPCL currently holds 32 days of LPG inventory, including supplies in transit.
The company has also diversified liquefied natural gas (LNG) procurement by increasing spot purchases from the US, Oman and West Africa.

articles.title: Rubio to host G20 Foreign Ministers’ meet in Atlanta on Oct 30-31
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: U.S. President Donald Trump is scheduled to host the G20 Leaders’ Summit in Miami on December 14-15

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will host the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting this weekend in Atlanta to strengthen efforts to advance practical cooperation on shared economic and security challenges, thereby setting the stage for the leaders’ meeting in December.
External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar is scheduled to attend the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Atlanta on October 30-31.

“Under President Trump's leadership, the United States is returning the G20 to its core economic mission of driving growth, strengthening economic security, and delivering results for the American people,” the Department of State said in a statement.
It said Mr. Rubio will convene Foreign Ministers from the world’s leading economies to advance practical cooperation on shared economic and security challenges.

“Throughout the ministerial, the United States will work with G20 partners to address geopolitical crises contributing to global economic shocks, including threats to freedom of navigation, energy and food security, and supply chains,” the State Department said.

It said global security and economic prosperity are inextricably linked, and these discussions will set the stage for U.S. President Trump’s G20 Leaders’ Summit and the broader economic agenda that leaders will tackle.

As a global hub of diplomacy, connectivity, and commerce, Atlanta offers the perfect backdrop for these discussions. U.S. President Donald Trump is scheduled to host the G20 Leaders’ Summit in Miami on December 14-15.

articles.title: Anthropic files for IPO as revenue jumps 14-fold to $16.3 billion in H1
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Claude maker reports $80.7 billion first-half net loss, largely due to valuation-related accounting charges; revenue from existing customers grows ninefold

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind Claude, has filed to go public in the United States, disclosing rapid revenue growth, expanding enterprise spending and the high cost of developing and running advanced AI models.

The company filed a registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on October 26. It intends to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol “ANT”. The number of shares to be offered and the price range have not yet been determined.
The public filing follows Anthropic’s confidential submission of a draft registration statement to the SEC on June 1, 2026. The proposed IPO remains subject to regulatory review.

The company reported more than 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in revenue over the preceding 12 months as of September 30, up from more than 950 a year earlier. More than 1,900 customers generated at least $1 million, while approximately 250 generated at least $10 million.

For the six months ended June 30, 2026, Anthropic reported revenue of $16.3 billion, up from $1.16 billion in the corresponding period a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $80.7 billion from $13 billion, largely because of accounting expenses arising from changes in the estimated value of certain financing instruments as the company’s valuation rose.

Anthropic reported an operating loss of $693 million in the first half of 2026, compared with $2.14 billion a year earlier. However, using its own adjusted measure, which excludes certain expenses, the company reported operating income of $1.6 billion, with a margin of about 10%.

It reported $8.95 billion in computing and infrastructure expenses in the first half of 2026, reflecting the costs of developing and running advanced AI models. As of June 30, the company held $131.7 billion in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments, according to the filing.
ALSO WATCH Anthropic loses over $80 billion in first half of 2026

The prospectus flags risks including dependence on computing infrastructure providers, competition and the cost of developing increasingly capable AI models. Major cloud providers supply Anthropic with computing capacity and help distribute its products, while also developing competing AI services.

The filing also outlines a governance structure intended to protect Anthropic’s long-term public-benefit mission. An entity formed by its seven co-founders will hold a special share carrying 50.1% of general voting power, while the company’s Long-Term Benefit Trust will have the right to appoint a majority of the board. This would limit the ability of ordinary shareholders to influence corporate governance, even after the company lists publicly.
Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be offered or the proposed price range. The timing and terms of the IPO will depend on the regulatory process and market conditions.

articles.title: Russia says open to mini Ukraine ceasefires, but no letup in war
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: A ceasefire is to start in the southern Ukrainian city early October 27, brokered by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump after months of reports that residents faced dire food, water and medicine shortages

Russia said Monday (October 26, 2026) that it would not slow down its offensive on Ukraine despite upcoming U.S.-brokered talks on ending the conflict but that it could agree local "humanitarian" ceasefires.
The Kremlin said that it was open to short-term "humanitarian" ceasefires along the front line, ahead of a truce in the ravaged Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

A ceasefire is to start in the southern Ukrainian city early Tuesday (October 27), brokered by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump after months of reports that residents faced dire food, water and medicine shortages.
Asked whether Russia would consider more local truces, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters: "For humanitarian purposes, absolutely."
But Moscow vowed not to let up in the overall pace of the war, even as the sides prepare to restart stalled talks under U.S. mediation next month.
"The decision to resume trilateral talks does not imply any restrictions on combat operations," Mr. Peskov said.
"Our armed forces continue to carry out massive strikes on Ukraine's military-industrial complex," he added.

Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, hitting energy sites around major cities in what Kyiv says is a bid to plunge the country into cold and darkness throughout the winter.
Strikes last year left millions without heating or electricity with temperatures as low as -20C.
The two sides are to meet next month with U.S. envoys to discuss ways to end Europe's worst conflict since World War II.
Several previous rounds have failed to move the sides closer to a deal. Russia demands more territory in eastern Ukraine and sweeping military and political restrictions on Kyiv.
Ukraine and its allies say the demands are tantamount to a capitulation that would leave the country exposed to a future Russian attack.

articles.title: Mass outages in Sudan after RSF drones hit five power stations
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref, and one in White Nile state, "resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states", the official said on condition of anonymity

Sudan's Paramilitary Rapid Support Forces launched a coordinated drone attack Monday (October 26, 2026) against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country's east, a government official told AFP .

The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref, and one in White Nile state, "resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states", the official said on condition of anonymity.
All three states are controlled by the Sudanese army, which has since April 2023 been at war with its former ally, the RSF.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned that regular attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people, already facing the world's largest hunger crisis.
An AFP correspondent in Al-Jazira state reported the electricity had been out since 2 a.m. (0000 GMT).
Babiker Youssef, a resident of Al-Fao in Gedaref, said the power there had also been out since the same time.
"My son is diabetic; his insulin has to be stored in the fridge," he told AFP over the phone, scared he would not be able to replace the medication if it spoils.
"We have no idea when the power will come back," he added.

Electricity has been cut for days at a time after past Paramilitary drone strikes on power stations and hydroelectric dams, compounding the suffering of nearly 20 million people facing extreme hunger.
Sudan's war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks from across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.
In the first three weeks of October alone, drone strikes killed over 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a UN tally.
Africa's third-largest country, home to an estimated 50 million people, has been ravaged by the war, which aid workers estimate has killed more than 200,000 people.

articles.title: Plant-based meat yields higher share of absorbable protein than traditional meat: study
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Laboratory tests show higher protein bioavailability in five plant-based products than in their chicken counterparts; researchers caution further studies needed to assess health benefits

While plant-derived kababs may still struggle to replicate the taste and texture of meat from a tandoori joint, they may contain relatively more protein in a form that the body can absorb, according to a study presented on Monday (October 26, 2026).

In a collaboration between the CSIR–Institute of Himalayan Bioresource Technology (CSIR-IHBT), Palampur, and the Good Food Institute (GFI) India, a non-profit that promotes alternative proteins such as plant-based, fermentation-derived and cultivated meat, scientists investigated whether protein bioavailability (meaning protein in a form that’s nutritively useful to the body) of traditional meat was the same as that of plant-based meat.

Tests on five cooked plant-based products — two burger patties, a nugget and two seekh kebabs — showed higher bioavailability percentages than their chicken counterparts, according to the findings presented at a press conference on Monday (October 26). The plant-based kebabs scored 80.8% and 86.1% against 38.8% for chicken. The nugget scored 61.2% against 43.4%, and the patties recorded about 57% and 58% against 21.2%.

The findings do not mean plant-based meat is healthier, but only that they are nutritively comparable, as ‘healthier’ is a subjective term, Dr. Padma Ishwarya, senior scientist at GFI India, told The Hindu . “It’s too much of a vague term. It’s too broad a term…for health, we need to do further studies.”

The chicken products held more crude protein and released more amino acids, the building blocks of protein, during digestion, and Dr. Ishwarya said more products and samples would be tested in the next phase.

The work has not yet been published as a journal paper. “It is a report that is hosted on our website, but it is very much peer-reviewed,” Dr. Ishwarya said in a conversation with The Hindu . Two experts reviewed it, she said, and it was an overview and that detailed manuscripts would follow.

The team used an in vitro method that simulated digestion in a laboratory. Samples went through a two-minute salivary phase, then a stomach phase with digestive enzymes at pH 2 to 3, and then an intestinal phase. The method follows INFOGEST, an internationally harmonised protocol, Dr. Ishwarya said.

The team added an ultrafiltration membrane chosen to mimic the pore size of the human intestine. Whatever passed through the membrane was deemed bioavailable, and only free amino acids were measured. Each sample was adjusted to start with 40 milligrammes of protein.

Animal studies remain the gold standard, she said, but are tedious and require ethical clearances. The simulated method is faster and more reproducible. The team plans to conduct tests across laboratories next year so that NABL-accredited labs can use the method.

Plant-based meat, Dr. Ishwarya said, is made “specifically for biomimicking animal-derived meat”, unlike crisps or cereals, which are plant-based foods. It is made from soya, pea or wheat gluten, mostly soya, and shaped by extrusion, a process in which material is pushed through a die under heat and pressure. She said it contains no synthetic chemicals beyond ingredients such as spices and texturisers.

The study examined only protein. An earlier analysis in 2024 of about 120 products in the Indian market, she said, found that saturated fat and sodium levels were comparable to those in animal-derived products, leaving room for reduction. Plant-based products also supplied dietary fibre, which animal-derived products do not.

articles.title: Indian publishers contest Modi government’s privacy law
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The October 6 lawsuit, being ‌reported for the first time and due to be heard on October 27, 2026, is the most high-profile challenge to the government’s privacy ‌law

A group of 21 news publishers has challenged the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 , India’s privacy law, in court, arguing it would trample investigative work and let the government identify journalists’ sources, documents show.

Prime ​Minister Narendra Modi’s government announced the implementation of the law in 2025 to protect the digital personal data of ⁠users, raising compliance requirements for platforms like Meta and Google. The publishers have said that since media outlets were not exempt, the law was an invasion of press freedom.

Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having ‌a written carve-out for journalists like in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) said in a confidential filing at the Supreme Court, reviewed by Reuters .

The October 6, 2026 lawsuit, being ‌reported for the first time and due to be heard on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), is the most high-profile challenge to the government’s privacy ‌law. ⁠Until now, only free speech activists and a group of smaller news outlets had challenged it.

It also ⁠marks an unusual challenge to the government from businesses headed by Mr. Ambani and Mr. Adani, who Opposition parties allege are close to Mr. Modi and get favourable treatment — charges the businesses and the government vehemently deny.
DNPA and the media groups did not respond to requests for comment from Reuters , and neither did the IT Ministry.

The publishers are demanding that most of the ‌law’s contentious provisions, which kick in from May 2027, be quashed. They are arguing that the law could force a journalist to get prior consent from a person they want to investigate and force publishers to erase stories. They also say powers granted by the law to demand information could expose reporters’ sources.

The law would “render investigative journalism a benign and neutered recorder ‌of events,” the 698-page filing said. The provisions “constitute pre-censorship which is anathema to any democracy worth its name”.

The lawsuit ​comes amid accusations of declining press freedom in India since Mr. Modi took office in 2014. Critics say many mainstream media outlets have not done enough to scrutinise the Modi government.
India’s ranking in Reporters Without Borders’ World ⁠Press Freedom Index fell to 157 th out of 180 countries this year, from 140 th in 2014 — but the government rejects the rankings.

Modi government says it respects press freedom and says India, which has a “vibrant press and media ecosystem” of hundreds of newspapers and TV ‌channels, does not need validation from foreign bodies.

DNPA’s members include Mr. Ambani’s Network18 , which has seven digital news platforms, Mr. Adani’s NDTV and other marquee media groups, including The Hindu, the Indian Express and Times Internet , which is part of the Times of India group, publisher of India’s largest-selling English-language daily.

articles.title: The Hindu Group, Cancer Institute launch book on comprehensive cancer care
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Cancer 360 examines detection, treatment, rehabilitation and palliation

The Hindu Group, in association with the Cancer Institute (WIA), Adyar, launched Cancer 360: Overview of Detection, Treatment, Palliation , a book examining cancer care from prevention and early detection to treatment, rehabilitation and palliative care. The book was launched at The Hindu office in Chennai.

N. Ram, director of The Hindu Group, launched the book alongside Suresh Nambath, editor of The Hindu . Mr. Ram handed over the first copy to E. Hemanth Raj, executive vice-chairman of Cancer Institute.

Speaking at the launch, Mr. Ram emphasised the importance of making advanced cancer care accessible and affordable. He highlighted the institute’s work in providing treatment to those who need it most and stressed the need to ensure that advances in cancer care reach patients facing barriers to treatment.

Dr. Hemanth Raj spoke about the need to translate advances in cancer research, much of which takes place in the West, into practical interventions in local settings. He also highlighted the institute’s charitable programmes, supported by donations, to help patients access treatment and facilities, and its plans to expand cancer care to reach more patients.
Arvind Krishnamurthy, professor of surgical oncology at Cancer Institute, stressed the need for continued research to improve cancer care and develop better treatments.

The book also addresses care beyond treatment. Mahalakshmi Rangabashyam Shetty, ENT surgeon and lecturer in the Department of Surgical Oncology at the institute, spoke about individualised treatment plans developed through multidisciplinary consultations. She also highlighted the need to tailor exercise and nutrition regimens to individual patients, alongside supportive services such as hospice care.

Surendran Veeraiah, professor and head of the Department of Regional Cancer Centre (RCTC), Cancer Institute, emphasised the importance of psychological support and allied services. He said the book could help make technical information on comprehensive cancer care accessible to more people.

The book features contributions from experts across oncology and allied disciplines. Its chapters cover multidisciplinary tumour boards, psychological care, onco-physiotherapy, palliative care, cancer research, speech and swallowing rehabilitation, early detection, precision treatment, pathology, nutrition and healthcare quality.

articles.title: Over 100 mills commence sugar production
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: As many as 107 sugar mills have commenced sugarcane crushing for the marketing season that started on October 1, 2026, according to the Indian Sugar & Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association.
Sugar mills in Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, and Uttar Pradesh have commenced crushing operations.

The previous sugar season that ended on September 30 closed with approximately 36 lakh tonnes of carryover stocks, providing a base for meeting domestic consumption requirements. As of 25 October 2026, sugar production during the current 2026–27 season had reached approximately four lakh tonnes, compared with just about 0.6 lakh tonnes on the corresponding date last year.

The Government has extended the duty-free raw sugar import window and introduced stockholding limits. These measures, together with available carryover stocks and the commencement of fresh production, contribute to ensuring adequate sugar availability for domestic consumption during the festive period, it said.

articles.title: Dubious retreat: on the National Medical Commission and its MSMER
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The National Medical Commission must not be seen as lax on regulation

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has denotified and withdrawn its 2023 Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations (MSMER), diminishing the framework of penalties vis-à-vis educational standards and infrastructure at medical colleges. The move is noteworthy as the MSMER provided for fines of up to ₹5 lakh on faculty members and administrators for submitting false information. Fortunately, the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) retains the power to fine errant institutions up to ₹1 crore under the 2023 Establishment of Medical Institutions, Assessment and Rating Regulations. MSMER was lauded for its intention to crack down on the deep-seated corruption and malpractice in medical colleges, particularly over ‘ghost faculty’ and ‘ghost patients’. The NMC’s justification is that MSMER also introduced a parallel mechanism allowing undergraduate and postgraduate boards to evaluate institutions, stepping on the MARB’s toes. However, why the NMC scrapped MSMER wholesale is unclear. The 2023 Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations remain in force and include a provision to fine individual faculty members at postgraduate medical colleges. Non-compliance among medical colleges is not uncommon and seldom nipped in the bud, even as the number of medical seats swells while the transparency of the medical education system has not improved.

Notwithstanding the provision to fine individuals at postgraduate centres, the MARB and the NMC can only penalise institutions, which is harder and risks creating a perverse incentive to accommodate rather than punish, and could mitigate the fear that keeps administrators honest. MSMER also specified timelines to appeal penalties. Although the MARB regulations retain the appeal processes, their 15-day deadline could conflict with the 60-day period under the NMC Act, potentially creating legal disputes that delay penal action. There is also a telling incident. ✍️ Editorial & Opinion 📅 26 Oct 2026 • IN-APP NEWSPAPER PRINT EDITION

Dubious retreat: on the National Medical Commission and its MSMER

🎯 Exam Relevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary

The National Medical Commission must not be seen as lax on regulation

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has denotified and withdrawn its 2023 Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations (MSMER), diminishing the framework of penalties vis-à-vis educational standards and infrastructure at medical colleges. The move is noteworthy as the MSMER provided for fines of up to ₹5 lakh on faculty members and administrators for submitting false information. Fortunately, the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) retains the power to fine errant institutions up to ₹1 crore under the 2023 Establishment of Medical Institutions, Assessment and Rating Regulations. MSMER was lauded for its intention to crack down on the deep-seated corruption and malpractice in medical colleges, particularly over ‘ghost faculty’ and ‘ghost patients’. The NMC’s justification is that MSMER also introduced a parallel mechanism allowing undergraduate and postgraduate boards to evaluate institutions, stepping on the MARB’s toes. However, why the NMC scrapped MSMER wholesale is unclear. The 2023 Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations remain in force and include a provision to fine individual faculty members at postgraduate medical colleges. Non-compliance among medical colleges is not uncommon and seldom nipped in the bud, even as the number of medical seats swells while the transparency of the medical education system has not improved.

Notwithstanding the provision to fine individuals at postgraduate centres, the MARB and the NMC can only penalise institutions, which is harder and risks creating a perverse incentive to accommodate rather than punish, and could mitigate the fear that keeps administrators honest. MSMER also specified timelines to appeal penalties. Although the MARB regulations retain the appeal processes, their 15-day deadline could conflict with the 60-day period under the NMC Act, potentially creating legal disputes that delay penal action. There is also a telling incident. As part of a proceeding under the RTI Act, the Central Information Commission revealed last year that the NMC had stated in 2024 that MARB had neither formally assessed nor rated medical colleges and that its standard forms need not be made public. In a revised reply in October 2025, it said the responding NMC officer’s records did not include any of the corresponding reports. However, the 2023 MARB regulations require the Board to publish its latest annual assessment results. If the NMC withdrew MSMER because the powers thereunder also exist elsewhere, the public deserves to know whether the powers are also being exercised and whether the outcomes are as publicly accessible as intended. Unless the NMC has satisfactory answers for all these lacunae, the withdrawal will appear less like simplification and more like regulatory relaxation.

articles.title: A final surge: on Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s triumph in Brazil
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Lula is the resistance to U.S. imperial ambitions in South America

At one point, it seemed almost impossible for Brazil’s 80-year-old President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to turn the tide after finishing second to Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of elections on October 4. In Brazil’s history, no candidate who has finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidential run-off. Most of the candidates who dropped out after the first round were from the right. Flávio’s Liberal Party cemented its position in both houses of Congress, while right-wing candidates won several provincial elections. But Lula, a former trade unionist and organiser, who lost a finger in an accident as a teenager, was not ready to give up. Lula and his Workers’ Party identified campaign weaknesses, shifted their attention to economic issues, promised growth and welfare, and persuaded more voters to turn out for Sunday’s run-off. Lula won 51.7% of the vote against Flávio’s 48.2%, a greater lead than his victory against Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio’s father, four years ago. Over the weeks, Lula turned the right-wing’s gains in the first round against it, highlighting the threats that a Bolsonaro victory could pose to democracy and civil rights. Flávio’s campaign pledge to free his father — he is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn Lula’s 2022 victory, and impeach Supreme Court judges — only heightened the concerns of voters outside the right wing, who rallied behind a familiar face.

Lula unleashed a social media campaign to mobilise younger voters. A WhatsApp channel called ‘Lula’s Army’ with 11 million followers spread his message of continuity. He also announced plans to expand a cash payout scheme for the poor, a new debt relief package and entrepreneur-friendly measures. In the northeast, the Workers’ Party’s stronghold, he gained nearly three million votes and made considerable gains in the working-class neighbourhoods of big cities, including São Paulo. A relatively stable economic record, marked by growth and falling unemployment over the past three and a half years, also lent credibility to Lula’s appeal. His victory bucks the recent trend in South America, where Washington-aligned right-wing and conservative forces have gained ground. While Lula offers predictable stability and social and economic inclusiveness, he could also be, as the President of South America’s largest economy, a voice of resistance to Donald Trump’s imperial ambitions. At the same time, Lula will have to work with a right-wing-controlled Congress to advance his agenda. He should seek to build legislative consensus while focusing on addressing the economic challenges of Brazil, which remains one of the most unequal major world economies.

articles.title: Peace for progress: on the SCO, regional cooperation, the fight against terror
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Economic objectives can be met only in a stable security environment

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh’s address at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Tajikistan, on Tuesday marks another significant occasion since Operation Sindoor (2025) when India has used the multilateral forum to raise the issue of terrorism, including cross-border terrorism from Pakistan. He said that regional cooperation cannot be meaningful if countries approached terrorism selectively. Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar’s presence added significance to the remarks, underscoring New Delhi’s diplomatic challenge within an organisation whose members have divergent strategic interests and security priorities. India has consistently argued that terrorism cannot be divorced from the broader agenda of regional peace, economic integration and development. By calling on SCO member-states to dismantle the ecosystem of terrorism, he reiterated that the threat must be addressed at its source rather than treated as an isolated security challenge. The intervention follows India’s refusal to endorse the joint statement at the 2025 SCO Defence Ministers’ meet in Qingdao, China. New Delhi had objected to a draft that failed to reflect its concerns over cross-border and Pakistan-sponsored terrorism, including the Pahalgam attack (2025), while referring to militant activities in Balochistan. India maintained that such an approach would undermine the organisation’s credibility by overlooking the threat it had brought before its members.

The SCO has the potential to advance regional stability, trade and connectivity instead of becoming another source of strategic friction. Yet, its effectiveness will remain limited if political disagreements prevent members from developing a common approach to security threats. India’s position is not that cooperation on trade, culture, connectivity and development must be suspended until every security dispute is resolved. Rather, these objectives cannot be met independently of a stable security environment. Economic corridors require predictable borders, investors need confidence in the rule of law, and transport networks must be violence- and disruption-free. Connectivity projects such as the International North-South Transport Corridor and the development of Chabahar Port offer Central Asia connectivity with wider markets. Their long-term value, however, depends on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, alongside conditions that allow goods, capital and people to move freely. The SCO’s challenge is to translate its stated commitment to combating terrorism into practical cooperation through intelligence-sharing, action against terror financing, disruption of recruitment networks and the denial of safe havens to terrorist groups. While retaining its principle against terrorism, India should lead efforts to achieve more regional cooperation in tackling it.

The SCO’s challenge is to translate its stated commitment to combating terrorism into practical cooperation through intelligence-sharing, action against terror financing, disruption of recruitment networks and the denial of safe havens to terrorist groups. While retaining its principle against terrorism, India should lead efforts to achieve more regional cooperation in tackling it.

articles.title: Bitter and sweet: on FSSAI draft restrictions, added sugars in infant foods
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The FSSAI must expand restrictions to cover all added sugars in infant foods

The Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2020 currently allow manufacturers to add sucrose and fructose, provided their combined total does not exceed 20% of the carbohydrates in a product intended for infants aged 0-6 months. In a draft proposal, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has pitched to eliminate this allowance — in line with WHO’s recommendation to have infants breastfeed exclusively for the first six months, followed by nutritionally adequate complementary foods avoiding added sugars until 24 months. While corporations have defended sugary formulations as abiding by the Codex Alimentarius, public health experts have repeatedly described their decision to sell infant foods with added sugar as nutritional dumping. Adding sugar has often been a commercial strategy, as it serves as a cheap bulking agent, improves palatability and encourages repeat purchases. WHO’s nutrient and promotion profile model for baby foods in 2022 also identified sweet purées and products in which fruits released sugars during processing as concerns. While the FSSAI’s draft proposal is a step in the right direction, stopping here would allow manufacturers to replace sucrose with another sweetening ingredient. It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.

articles.title: NDA secures six of nine urban local bodies in Kadapa district unopposed
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: In a significant development, the TDP-led NDA has secured the chairperson posts in six urban local bodies in Kadapa district, considered a stronghold of the YSR family, even before the elections. Candidates representing the ruling coalition have been unanimously elected to the posts.

Despite the disruption caused by the revised schedule announced by the State Election Commission (SEC) following a direction from the Supreme Court, the ruling coalition focused on securing the unanimous election of as many ward councillors and chairpersons as possible.

Gorla Madhulatha (Yerraguntla), Nandyala Raghava Reddy (Proddatur), Dhanapala Jaganmohan Raju (Mydukur), Somasila Divyateja (Badvel), Gongalireddy Swapna (Kamalapuram) and Dontham Gayatri (Rajampet) have been elected unopposed as chairpersons.

In Rajampet, 14 NDA candidates and an independent candidate were declared elected unanimously. In Pulivendula, however, YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) president Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy’s aunt, Y.S. Prameela, is locked in a close contest with TDP candidate T. Geetha Kumari.

Several YSRCP councillor candidates withdrew from the contest even in municipalities such as Pulivendula, Rajampet and Proddatur, where the party wielded considerable influence in the past. Rachamallu Ramadevi, wife of YSRCP State spokesperson and former MLA Rachamallu Sivaprasad Reddy, also withdrew her candidature at the last moment, citing personal reasons.
As a result, elections will be held only in the Kadapa Municipal Corporation and the Jammalamadugu and Pulivendula municipalities, as per the revised schedule.

In Kadapa, TDP zonal coordinator R. Srinivasa Reddy and MLA R. Madhavi Reddy are campaigning vigorously for mayoral candidate Matli Suvarna, promising to improve basic amenities, including drinking water supply, sanitation and public safety.

articles.title: Owner, mahout booked for neglected elephant in Kozhikode
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Forest officials find signs of severe malnutrition and chain-related injuries during an inspection at Ekarool near Unnikulam
The Forest department has registered a case against the owner and mahout of an elephant, Cheriyaparambath Gopalan, for allegedly failing to provide the animal with adequate food and care.
The action followed an inspection by a team of forest officials and veterinary doctors at the owner’s residence in Ekarool near Unnikulam in Kozhikode district.
Blood samples collected from the elephant were sent to Pookode Veterinary College for analysis. The report indicated severe malnutrition and inadequate care.

During the inspection, officials found that the elephant was not being fed the prescribed diet recorded in its care register. The inadequate feeding had left the animal severely weakened, they said. Injuries and sores caused by chains rubbing against its legs were also found.

There were allegations that the elephant had been used for timber-hauling work despite its poor health.The elephant was placed under the care of social forestry officials and veterinary doctors, who are overseeing its feeding and treatmen.

The owner, meanwhile, said the elephant had been receiving treatment from a doctor in Thrissur because of its weakness. He claimed that it had last been taken to a temple procession during the previous Thrissur Pooram and had not been used for timber hauling or other strenuous work in recent months.

articles.title: BJP slams Kharge over ‘indecent’ remarks on PM Modi
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: BJP leaders said Mallikarjun Kharge’s language was “indecent and unparliamentary” and showed the “desperation and frustration” within the Congress party

Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge’s remarks at a Patna event on Sunday (October 25, 2026), in which he dragged Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s late father, triggered a sharp reaction from senior Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leaders, who accused the principal Opposition, under Rahul Gandhi’s leadership, of increasingly resorting to personal attacks against Mr. Modi and his family.
Criticising the “ Modi ka baap bhi jayega [even Modi’s father will go]” comment, Union Home Minister Amit Shah said Mr. Kharge has “torn apart all norms of decorum”.

“This is not the first time that the Congress party has used abusive language against Modi ji or his family,” he said, accusing the party of having hurled insults at the Prime Minister’s mother, calling him a “merchant of death”, and mocking his poverty by addressing him as a “chaiwala” in the past.

“Under Rahul Gandhi’s leadership, the Congress party keeps crossing the limits of indecency every day,” he said, alleging that repeated electoral defeats over the past 12 years had bred “desperation and frustration” within the party.

कांग्रेस अध्यक्ष मल्लिकार्जुन खरगे ने आज पटना में मोदी जी के पिताजी के बारे में अभद्र टिप्पणी कर सारी मर्यादाएँ तार-तार कर दी हैं। यह पहली बार नहीं है, जब कांग्रेस पार्टी ने मोदी जी या उनके परिवार को अपशब्द कहे हों। कभी उनकी पूजनीय माताजी के विषय में अपशब्द कहे, कभी उन्हें 'मौत का सौदागर' कहा, तो कभी 'चायवाला' कहकर उनकी गरीबी का उपहास उड़ाया। राहुल गांधी के नेतृत्व में कांग्रेस पार्टी हर रोज अभद्रता की सीमाएँ पार करती जा रही है। बीते 12 वर्षों में लगातार मिल रही चुनावी हार से कांग्रेस पार्टी में हताशा व निराशा इतनी बढ़ चुकी है कि अब उसके पास न कोई नीति बची है, न कोई मुद्दा, बस गाली-गलौज की राजनीति बची है। जनता के बीच जनाधार खो चुकी कांग्रेस, अब अपने कार्यकर्ताओं में भी आधार खोती जा रही है। जब-जब इन्होंने मोदी जी या उनके परिवार पर घृणित टिप्पणियाँ की हैं, तब-तब जनता ने कांग्रेस को करारा जवाब दिया है।

Terming Mr. Kharge’s language “indecent and unparliamentary”, BJP chief Nitin Nabin said: “There is a certain dignity to political opposition as well, but dragging the departed family members into speeches from public platforms has now become the real ‘culture’ of Rahul Gandhi and the whole Opposition. This is not Kharge ji’s personal statement, but a reflection of the entire Congress party’s lack of decorum in its thinking.”

He said that in a democracy, opponents must not “cross the bounds of propriety”, and the people will respond to such politics. “The Congress must realise that the trust of the people cannot be won through a politics of hatred and humiliation. The people of the country will surely deliver their response to such petty politics through democratic means,” he said.

आज पटना में कांग्रेस अध्यक्ष मल्लिकार्जुन खड़गे द्वारा देश के माननीय प्रधानमंत्री श्री नरेंद्र मोदी जी के प्रति जिस प्रकार की अमर्यादित और असंसदीय भाषा का प्रयोग किया गया है, वह कांग्रेस के वैचारिक दिवालियापन को दर्शाता है। राजनीतिक विरोध की भी एक गरिमा होती है, लेकिन सार्वजनिक मंच से स्वर्गीय परिजनों को भाषणों में घसीटना ही अब राहुल गांधी और समूचे विपक्ष का असली 'संस्कार' बन चुका है। यह खड़गे जी का व्यक्तिगत बयान नहीं, बल्कि पूरी कांग्रेस की शिष्टाचार-विहीन सोच का प्रकटीकरण है। जब विपक्ष के पास देश के विकास, नीति और जनकल्याणकारी योजनाओं पर बहस करने के लिए कोई ठोस मुद्दा नहीं बचता, तो वे इसी प्रकार की हताशा और व्यक्तिगत आक्षेपों का सहारा लेते हैं। देश की जनता इस अमर्यादित राजनीति को भली-भांति देख रही है और समय आने पर इसका करारा जवाब देगी।

BJP slams Kharge over ‘indecent’ remarks on PM Modi

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes

BJP leaders said Mallikarjun Kharge’s language was “indecent and unparliamentary” and showed the “desperation and frustration” within the Congress party

Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge’s remarks at a Patna event on Sunday (October 25, 2026), in which he dragged Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s late father, triggered a sharp reaction from senior Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leaders, who accused the principal Opposition, under Rahul Gandhi’s leadership, of increasingly resorting to personal attacks against Mr. Modi and his family.

Criticising the “ Modi ka baap bhi jayega [even Modi’s father will go]” comment, Union Home Minister Amit Shah said Mr. Kharge has “torn apart all norms of decorum”.

“This is not the first time that the Congress party has used abusive language against Modi ji or his family,” he said, accusing the party of having hurled insults at the Prime Minister’s mother, calling him a “merchant of death”, and mocking his poverty by addressing him as a “chaiwala” in the past.

“Under Rahul Gandhi’s leadership, the Congress party keeps crossing the limits of indecency every day,” he said, alleging that repeated electoral defeats over the past 12 years had bred “desperation and frustration” within the party.

कांग्रेस अध्यक्ष मल्लिकार्जुन खरगे ने आज पटना में मोदी जी के पिताजी के बारे में अभद्र टिप्पणी कर सारी मर्यादाएँ तार-तार कर दी हैं। यह पहली बार नहीं है, जब कांग्रेस पार्टी ने मोदी जी या उनके परिवार को अपशब्द कहे हों। कभी उनकी पूजनीय माताजी के विषय में अपशब्द कहे, कभी उन्हें 'मौत का सौदागर' कहा, तो कभी 'चायवाला' कहकर उनकी गरीबी का उपहास उड़ाया। राहुल गांधी के नेतृत्व में कांग्रेस पार्टी हर रोज अभद्रता की सीमाएँ पार करती जा रही है। बीते 12 वर्षों में लगातार मिल रही चुनावी हार से कांग्रेस पार्टी में हताशा व निराशा इतनी बढ़ चुकी है कि अब उसके पास न कोई नीति बची है, न कोई मुद्दा, बस गाली-गलौज की राजनीति बची है। जनता के बीच जनाधार खो चुकी कांग्रेस, अब अपने कार्यकर्ताओं में भी आधार खोती जा रही है। जब-जब इन्होंने मोदी जी या उनके परिवार पर घृणित टिप्पणियाँ की हैं, तब-तब जनता ने कांग्रेस को करारा जवाब दिया है।

Terming Mr. Kharge’s language “indecent and unparliamentary”, BJP chief Nitin Nabin said: “There is a certain dignity to political opposition as well, but dragging the departed family members into speeches from public platforms has now become the real ‘culture’ of Rahul Gandhi and the whole Opposition. This is not Kharge ji’s personal statement, but a reflection of the entire Congress party’s lack of decorum in its thinking.”

He said that in a democracy, opponents must not “cross the bounds of propriety”, and the people will respond to such politics. “The Congress must realise that the trust of the people cannot be won through a politics of hatred and humiliation. The people of the country will surely deliver their response to such petty politics through democratic means,” he said.

आज पटना में कांग्रेस अध्यक्ष मल्लिकार्जुन खड़गे द्वारा देश के माननीय प्रधानमंत्री श्री नरेंद्र मोदी जी के प्रति जिस प्रकार की अमर्यादित और असंसदीय भाषा का प्रयोग किया गया है, वह कांग्रेस के वैचारिक दिवालियापन को दर्शाता है। राजनीतिक विरोध की भी एक गरिमा होती है, लेकिन सार्वजनिक मंच से स्वर्गीय परिजनों को भाषणों में घसीटना ही अब राहुल गांधी और समूचे विपक्ष का असली 'संस्कार' बन चुका है। यह खड़गे जी का व्यक्तिगत बयान नहीं, बल्कि पूरी कांग्रेस की शिष्टाचार-विहीन सोच का प्रकटीकरण है। जब विपक्ष के पास देश के विकास, नीति और जनकल्याणकारी योजनाओं पर बहस करने के लिए कोई ठोस मुद्दा नहीं बचता, तो वे इसी प्रकार की हताशा और व्यक्तिगत आक्षेपों का सहारा लेते हैं। देश की जनता इस अमर्यादित राजनीति को भली-भांति देख रही है और समय आने पर इसका करारा जवाब देगी।

articles.title: Yamunotri, Kedarnath receive season’s first snowfall
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Pilgrims at Yamunotri were thrilled to witness the snowfall, with devotees who had arrived to seek the blessings of Goddess Yamuna taking the opportunity to enjoy the natural scenery amid the falling snow

The season's first snowfall at the Yamunotri shrine in Uttarakhand on Sunday (October 25, 2026) brought cheer to pilgrims visiting the temple, while Kedarnath also witnessed snowfall as the Char Dham Yatra entered its final phase.
Vinit Posti, a specially invited member of the Shri Kedarnath-Badrinath Temple Committee, appealed to pilgrims to carry all essential medicines and exercise caution during their journey.

Pilgrims at Yamunotri were thrilled to witness the snowfall, with devotees who had arrived to seek the blessings of Goddess Yamuna taking the opportunity to enjoy the natural scenery amid the falling snow.
Girish Uniyal, secretary of the Panch Panda Samiti, said pilgrims were visibly excited by the season's first snowfall.
"For some, it was their first time witnessing snowfall from such close quarters, leaving them absolutely overjoyed," he said.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) had forecast very light to light rain or snowfall at isolated places in Uttarkashi, Rudraprayag, Bageshwar, Chamoli and Pithoragarh districts of Uttarakhand on Sunday.

A surge in pilgrim arrivals during the final phase of the summer Char Dham Yatra has brought renewed activity to Yamunotri shrine, offering relief and optimism to local business owners whose livelihoods depend on the pilgrimage.
Around 6,000 pilgrims reached Yamunotri Dham on Saturday to offer prayers and seek the blessings of Goddess Yamuna.
Sunil Uniyal, secretary of the Yamunotri Temple Committee, said pilgrims from various parts of the country were arriving at the shrine during the final leg of the summer pilgrimage.
"This influx has has also proven beneficial for those involved in the Char Dham Yatra trade," he said.
The portals of Yamunotri will close for the six-month winter season on November 11, the auspicious occasion of Bhai Dooj, Uniyal said.
During winter, devotees will be able to seek the blessings of Goddess Yamuna at the Yamuna Temple in Kharsali.

articles.title: Kalaburagi’s GI-tagged tur dal wins PM’s praise after export to Maldives
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Kalaburagi’s GI-tagged tur dal has made its way to the international market, giving a boost to the Centre’s ‘Vocal for Local’ initiative. Prime Minister Narendra Modi highlighted the export of the region’s tur dal to the Maldives in his 139th episode of ‘Mann Ki Baat’, cheering farmers and the district’s agricultural sector.

Referring to the growing preference for indigenous products during the festive season, Mr. Modi said locally made goods were increasingly finding markets overseas. He said makhana from Purnia in Bihar was reaching Greece, and tur dal from Kalaburagi in Karnataka was being exported to the Maldives, pointing to new international market opportunities for Indian farmers.

Ramesh Kadaganchi of Kalaburagi facilitated the export of 10 quintals of GI-tagged tur dal to the Maldives through a Pune-based company about two months ago. Farmers received prices around 30% higher than the prevailing market rate in connection with the consignment, according to information provided by the Agriculture Department.

The export is expected to improve market prospects for Kalaburagi’s tur dal, whose geographical indication (GI) tag recognises its association with the region. The overseas shipment of Kalaburagi’s tur dal marks a step towards expanding the product’s international reach and improving returns for farmers.

Kalaburagi’s agricultural produce and traditional food products have featured in the Prime Minister’s ‘Mann Ki Baat’ programme earlier as well. In a previous episode, Mr. Modi appreciated efforts to promote Kalaburagi’s ‘khadak rotti’ (crisp flatbread made of jowar flour) and expand its market.

The Agriculture Department is now looking to increase tur dal exports to other countries, including the United States, Canada and Australia. Samples have been sent to prospective overseas buyers, and the department is awaiting export orders, Kalaburagi Joint Director of Agriculture Samad Patel said.

articles.title: LS Speaker Om Birla meets counterparts from Cuba, Russia ahead of BRICS parliamentary forum meeting
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Cuba lobbying for support of its UNGA resolution against a crippling economic blockade imposed by the U.S.; India, Russia review parliamentary exchanges as they mark 80th anniversary of bilateral ties

Ahead of Cuba’s resolution against the U.S. blockade to be taken up by the UN General Assembly on October 27, the Caribbean nation intensified its diplomatic outreach to the Global South on Sunday (October 25, 2026), with the Vice President of Cuba’s National Assembly of People’s Power and the Council of State Mari Machado meeting Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla here.

Following the meeting with Ms. Machado, Mr. Birla said they had “discussed strengthening parliamentary exchanges, capacity-building and cooperation in healthcare and pharmaceuticals.” Cuba is participating in the BRICS Parliamentary Forum meeting as a partner country of the grouping.

This comes two days after Cuba’s ambassador to India Juan Carlos Marsan Aguilera accused the United States of carrying out a naval blockade that has created an acute energy crisis in his country. “Cuba is fully capable of defending itself. The U.S. is practising the Monroe Doctrine in our region,” Mr. Aguilera said, seeking support for Cuba’s UNGA resolution.

Mr. Birla also met the Chairman of the State Duma of Russia, Vyacheslav Volodin, on Saturday (October 24), to discuss bilateral ties. India and Russia are marking the 80th anniversary of their bilateral relationship and the two dignitaries carried out a review of parliament-level exchanges between the two countries against the backdrop of unfolding global and regional developments.

The Lok Sabha Speaker informed the Russian delegation about the steps taken to make parliamentary proceedings accessible in various Indian languages through Sansad Bhashini. According to a statement issued by the Parliament Secretariat, Mr. Birla highlighted the importance of using technology in making parliamentary functioning more accessible, efficient, and people-centric.

articles.title: How people’s genes are revealing why some languages are so unique
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: A new study measured how different neighbouring languages were from one another. The authors say that linguistic hotspots may offer glimpses into how human languages became more varied before large migrations and population movements reshaped much of the world

Hindi and Tamil differ in far more than just vocabulary . Languages differ in how they are organised, and these differences are not spread evenly around the world. In some regions, neighbouring languages like Basque and Spanish differ dramatically from one another. In others, they share many of the same features, like Tamil and Kannada.

A new study by researchers from Europe and Japan has found human history itself gives shape to the pattern. After analysing thousands of languages alongside genetic data from populations around the world, the researchers found that places that were relatively isolated for a long time tended to harbour more linguistic features. On the other hand, regions shaped by migration and sustained contact contained languages that were more alike.

“I was struck by the clarity of the signal,” Anna Graff, lead author of the study and a biological anthropologist at the University of Zurich, said. “In studies of human history and diversity, such clear global patterns are often difficult to find.”

Crucially, the researchers did not count the number of languages in a region. Instead, they measured how different neighbouring languages were from one another. Some languages placed verbs near the beginning of a sentence while others placed them at the end. Some distinguished between a hand and a finger with separate words while others used the same term for both.

A region where languages had more such differences was considered more linguistically diverse than one where languages shared many of the same traits — even if both regions had the same number of languages.

To investigate, the researchers assembled one of the largest datasets of its kind, combining information from more than 4,200 languages with genetic data from over 5,700 individuals representing 650 populations around the world. Then they divided the world into hundreds of roughly 500-km-wide hexagonal cells and calculated two measures for each: diversity of linguistic features found among languages spoken there and the genetic diversity of the local populations.
Thus they found that regions whose populations had been relatively isolated over long periods tended to have more diverse linguistic features.

The effect was modest. Imagine describing each language using a checklist of 333 characteristics. The difference associated with isolation was roughly equivalent to making about 11 items on the checklist vary substantially across the languages spoken in a region.
Yet the pattern proved remarkably persistent, appearing again and again, across statistical tests.

The researchers also tested if the pattern could be explained by other obvious factors. Languages spoken close together often influence one another while related languages can resemble one another because they inherited features from a common ancestor. Yet neither explanation fully accounted for the trend.

At first glance, the findings also seem counterintuitive. One might expect places with a long history of migration and population mixing to have more language patterns. But Dr. Graff and her colleagues argued that contact often has the opposite effect. As people move, trade, and interact, languages can borrow words, sounds, and grammatical features from one another, gradually becoming more alike.
Isolation allows languages to evolve independently, increasing the chances that they will grow more different over time.

articles.title: Brazil votes in tense Lula vs Bolsonaro runoff with U.S. influence over Latin America at stake
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Flávio Bolsonaro bested Mr. Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round of the election earlier this month, although more than 33 million voters out of nearly 160 million did not turn out

Brazilians began voting in Sunday's (October 25, 2026) polarising presidential election between incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro , a contest that will determine whether the U.S. will significantly expand its growing influence in Latin America.

Polls before Sunday's (October 25) vote showed the two candidates, who need more than 50% of the vote to become Brazil's next leader in January, in a neck-and-neck race. The election pits the left-of-centre veteran politician Mr. Lula against Mr. Bolsonaro, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump and the son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro .
Flávio Bolsonaro bested Mr. Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round of the election earlier this month. More than 33 million voters out of nearly 160 million did not turn out.
The difference between the two candidates is stark. Mr. Bolsonaro and Mr. Lula have opposing ideological views on issues ranging from U.S.-Brazil relations and climate change to social welfare.

A win for Mr. Bolsonaro would signify a pivot to the right by Latin America's most populous country and its largest economy in a year when Trump allies have notched victories in Chile, Peru and Colombia.
A victory for Mr. Lula would leave Brazil and Mexico, which is the region's second-most populous country and led by President Claudia Sheinbaum , with left-of-centre leaders.

In many ways, Brazil's runoff vote resembles a rematch between the country's two polarized political forces that trigger passion as much as loathing. Four years ago, Mr. Lula beat Mr. Bolsonaro's father by the narrowest margin since the country's return to democracy in 1985. Polls suggest that this election will be even closer.

Mr. Lula, who first governed the country between 2003 and 2010, has faced a tough reelection battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Flávio Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime approach the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to bring down food costs.

Both have been hit by corruption suspicions involving family members and allies, with Mr. Bolsonaro implicated in a sprawling scandal rocking Brazil. Mr. Lula spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were eventually annulled.

Mr. Bolsonaro's admission that he accepted about $12 million from disgraced former banker Daniel Vorcaro to produce a film on his father's life has cast a shadow over his campaign. He is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in connection with the case.

In the lead-up to the vote, Mr. Lula frequently portrayed Mr. Bolsonaro, whose father is under house arrest for attempting a coup, as a threat to democracy. Mr. Bolsonaro has promised to seek an amnesty for his father if elected.

The next President will name at least three Supreme Court justices out of 11 in his next term due to upcoming retirements. Mr. Bolsonaro has long taken aim at the country's top court — which has been rocked by a corruption scandal — and promised to push for judiciary reform.

articles.title: String theory pioneer Ashoke Sen wins Oskar Klein Medal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The Oskar Klein Medal is awarded by Stockholm University and the Nobel Committee for Physics of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences

Theoretical physicist Ashoke Sen has been awarded the 2026 Oskar Klein Medal , becoming the first Indian laureate to receive the honour, awarded by Stockholm University and the Nobel Committee for Physics of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.

The Medal recognises significant contributions to theoretical physics. Dr. Sen is the ICTS-Infosys Madhava Chair Professor at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences (ICTS), Bengaluru. He also delivered the memorial lecture accompanying the Medal in Stockholm on October 22, under the title ‘Gravity from Strings and Strings from Gravity’.

In his career, Dr. Sen has focused on string theory, which is the name of an attempt by physicists to describe matter and nature’s fundamental forces, including gravity, within a single framework called quantum gravity. Currently, they are split across two frameworks, quantum physics and relativity. String theory offers ways to reconcile them, but while it is mathematically a highly evolved theory, it has been unable to make predictions that can be confirmed with experiments using today’s technologies.

In the 1980s, Dr. Sen helped establish how the equations describing hypothetical strings moving through space could relate to the equations that describe the physical fields that surround it. In the 1990s, he helped show that two apparently different ways to describe physical forces were really equivalent, an idea called S-duality.
He also proposed three related ideas, together called the Sen conjectures, in 1999 that gave physicists new ways to understand the behaviour of the strings of string theory.

Dr. Sen graduated from Presidency College in Kolkata before going to IIT-Kanpur and thereon to earning his PhD from Stony Brook University, New York, in 1982. After working at institutions including the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in Mumbai and the Harish-Chandra Research Institute (HRI) in Prayagraj, he moved to ICTS in 2021. For his work, he has won the S.S. Bhatnagar Prize (1994), the Infosys Prize (2009), the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics (2012), and the Dirac Medal (2014).
He also received the Padma Shri in 2001 and the Padma Bhushan in 2013.

The impact of Dr. Sen’s contributions has exceeded their own ambit. In one 2014 interview, U.S. theoretical physicist Edward Witten — widely considered to be the greatest living mathematical physicist — called one of Dr. Sen’s papers “short but brilliant” and that it “convinced me that the duality had to be right”. Dr. Witten also said Dr. Sen’s findings had inspired work that paved the way for more breakthroughs in understanding how subatomic particles interact with each other.

He has also done important work on black holes. Physicists had long known that these enigmatic cosmic beasts had entropy but could not explain its origins in their physical theories. Dr. Sen developed mathematical methods to make sense of a black hole’s microscopic states in a way that could account for its observable, macroscopic characteristics.
Together, many physicists agree, his contributions have considerably advanced the theories physicists use to understand quantum gravity.

The Oskar Klein Medal and the accompanying Memorial Lectures were launched in 1988 to honour the Swedish physicist Oskar Klein (1894-1977). In 1926, Klein, building on the work of German mathematician Theodor Kaluza, explored whether electromagnetism and gravity could be described in a common framework by introducing an extra dimension of space. The result, known as Kaluza-Klein theory, exerted a significant influence on later attempts by physicists — including string theory — to unify these forces.

India in particular has an influential community of string theorists, especially at TIFR Mumbai, ICTS Bengaluru, HRI Prayagraj, and the Indian Institute of Science Education Research in Pune. Aside from Dr. Sen, the community’s notable members include Nabamita Banerjee, Shiraz Minwalla, Sunil Mukhi, P. Ramadevi, and Spenta Wadia.

articles.title: KSSP supports distribution of generic drug for SMA patients in Keralam
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad president C. Ramakrishnan and general secretary V. Manoj Kumar say that access to this medication is crucial for improving the quality of life and life expectancy of patients

The Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP) has supported the Kerala Health Department’s decision to provide a low-cost generic version of the drug Risdiplam to patients afflicted with Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a rare and threatening genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness.
In a statement, KSSP president C. Ramakrishnan and general secretary V. Manoj Kumar said that access to this medication is crucial for improving the quality of life and life expectancy of patients.
The statement from the pro-Left people’s science movement comes close on the heels of public health experts such as B. Ekbal, K.P. Aravindan, and V. Ramankutty endorsing the government’s stand.

The KSSP functionaries pointed out that Natco Pharma is an Indian pharmaceutical company that plays a key role in making affordable cancer treatments more accessible to the general public, both in India and in international markets. They claimed that the department’s decision is not merely aimed at saving public funds. It is a humanitarian responsibility to ensure that life-saving treatment is accessible to more SMA patients, they added.
